The relationship between angiosperm and bee richness probably reflects a combination of shared biogeographic drivers, such as area and climate, as well as ecological dependence, although the contribution of these factors cannot be separated here. However, the markedly higher baseline bee richness in Mediterranean-type islands at equivalent angiosperm richness is consistent with the hypothesis that temperature seasonality promotes bee specialization57. Seasonal climates can promote bee specialization through temporal resource partitioning while perhumid tropical systems, despite higher plant richness, may present ecological filters that limit bee diversity. Therefore, capturing more detailed information on the complex networks that wild bees form with native plants, and how they vary with island isolation and reduced colonization events, is crucial for developing more complete models of island biodiversity58,59 (reviewed in ref. 1). Yet recent evidence highlights that flowering plant communities may be reliant on bee pollinators when bee richness is comparatively low60. Consequently, we should not expect a simple, predictable relationship between plant and bee richness across islands of differing biomes, isolation and area.

Industry observers note that our study demonstrates that islands account for a substantial share of global bee diversity, including many species that evolved on islands and are endemic. We find that species richness and endemism are partly disconnected, highlighting that these two metrics capture distinct aspects of insular bee diversity. Richness peaks in mid-latitude, Mediterranean-type islands in the Northern Hemisphere, whereas peak endemism occurs in large tropical islands, with these differences being strongest for oceanic islands. These patterns are further supported by the biome-dependent relationship between angiosperm and bee richness, showing that although floral richness is a strong predictor of bee diversity across islands, it does not fully account for the differences in bee richness observed among biomes. Only a small percentage of island bee species have been assessed for extinction risk29,30, and this risk is probably tied to evolutionary distinctiveness rather than richness55. Therefore, our results suggest that conserving bees on islands requires prioritization of areas of unique evolutionary history, from large continental fragments such as Madagascar to remote oceanic archipelagos like the Hawaiian islands, over species richness alone.

Recent findings suggest that bees are particularly well suited as a model taxon for studying island biogeographical dynamics. They are pivotal pollinators that are closely linked to plant reproduction and ecosystem functioning22, and represent a taxonomically discrete group with an increasing availability of distributional and phylogenetic data. However, much remains to be explored in understanding the mechanisms behind the patterns of colonization and speciation, and the potential for new discoveries. The increasing availability of molecular phylogenies opens up new research avenues for addressing the evolutionary history of bees27. Combined with detailed distribution and trait data61, these resources make it possible to reconstruct historical patterns of colonization, extinction and speciation on islands. With the baseline established here, we lay the foundation for understanding the colonization, diversification and vulnerability of insect diversity on islands more broadly.

Sources indicate that we verified the presence of bees on islands on the basis of information available on Discover Life (https://www.discoverlife.org/) and more detailed and recently updated information, notably, for type locality and collection event data, extracted from source files for that resource21. These expert-vetted lists were filtered for island records and joined with spatial data to align species presence with island identifiers. The checklist data on Discover Life were collected from a variety of sources, including taxonomic revisions, primary species descriptions (including synonyms), verified human observations, and undigitized museum records. To avoid complications from historical boundary changes, species were recorded at the current state or country level. The data are available online as a matrix at the country level, with species-specific details provided for finer geographic scales. For further details on how the checklists were sourced see ref. 4. For islands not clearly associated with a specific country or state/province, additional sources were used to confirm species presence based on the broader political region. We then cross-referenced specimens with island-specific faunal checklists from the published literature; for example, when a species was known only from an archipelago we tried to determine its presence on specific islands within the archipelago. These included studies from Abd al Kuri and Socotra from the Socotra Archipelago65, the Azores including Corvo, Faial, Flores, Graciosa, Pico, Santa Maria, São Jorge, São Miguel and Terceira66, Balearic Islands including Ibiza, Mallorca and Menorca67, Bonaire68, Cabo Verde including Boa Vista, Brava, Sal, Santiago, Santo Antão, São Nicolau and São Vicente69, Cuba and East Grand Bahama70, Fiji52,71, Isla de Juventud72, Juan Fernández Islands73, Madeira Archipelago including Madeira, Porto Santo, and Deserto Grande and Selvagens Islands including Selvagem Grande74 and Madagascar75,76. European island checklists were extracted from the latest checklists for European species from Reverte et al.77 and included Åland islands, Great Britain, Ireland, Iceland, Faroe Islands, Malta, Corsica, Sardinia, Sicily, Crete, Cyprus and Isle of Man. We also included validated (Research Grade) iNaturalist records (up to December 2024) for all islands available from the initial checklists. Although these entries provide valuable data, a degree of taxonomic doubt remains, consequently, they have been labelled as uncertain within the final dataset pending further validation. The checklists for the Greek islands of Corfu and Rhodes were expanded with records from Rhodes78,79, Corfu80 and the personal collection of T. J. Wood. Recent additions to Corsica and Sardinia were also added81, as were the latest checklists of the Canary Islands82. Finally, the bee fauna of Tasmania was significantly adjusted due to recent taxonomic work on the Parasphecodes subgenus83. Names were cleaned using the synonym lists from Orr et al.4 and Dorey et al.84. In some cases, it was not possible to separate archipelago-level data into island records and some archipelagos were therefore retained in the dataset (for example, for the Solomon Islands).

To classify non-native species and calculate final island native species richness, we used Russo85 as a baseline, complemented by existing checklist information and expert opinion from J.S.A. Using the checklists, we calculated three measures of wild bee richness and endemism on islands. They included: (1) native species richness, calculated as the total number of unique native species included in the checklist for each island (or archipelago, as the case may be); (2) single-island endemism, calculated as the total number of species on the checklist only known from that island; (3) AE, calculated as the total number of species found only on that archipelago: this includes all SIEs.

According to recent reports, using the above checklists, we extracted a spatially explicit database of islands by matching the names from the checklist to those found in the global islands (greater than 1 km2 in area) database of Sayre et al.63. We extracted a vector shapefile of all islands for which we had any wild bee checklist information. In most cases we endeavoured to associate each checklist with a single island entity. In cases where a single name from the bee database is associated with multiple land masses, we extracted all the landmasses for subsequent calculations (for example, Sao Tome and Principe, Saint Vincent and Grenadines, Wallis and Futuna, Antigua and Barbuda, Saint Pierre and Miquelon, Saint Kitts and Nevis, and Solomon Islands). Duplicate island names and spatial mismatches were checked manually. Following this we harmonized the island names with the islands included in the Global Inventory of Floras and Traits (GIFT) database and extracted information on island area, isolation (distance to mainland), island category (oceanic, fragment or continental), archipelago and richness of angiosperms from GIFT (for more detail, see ref. 20). Islands in the GIFT database were categorized by geological origin into oceanic (volcanic islands and atolls), continental shelf (land-bridge), and complex origin/continental fragments. Categorizing islands into three discrete types is a necessary simplification. Certain cases, such as the tectonic uplift of Cyprus or continental fragments such as Rhodes, Newly introduced Caledonia and Seram that underwent periods of total submergence, represent intermediate states where biological isolation was prioritized over strict geological origin. Specifically, a lack of historical land-bridge connections was used to classify islands as oceanic in type. Of the final 305 islands, there were 207 oceanic islands, 25 fragment islands and 73 continental islands (see Supplementary Table 12 for a full breakdown by biome).

Species distribution data for 350,707 vascular plant species across 1,967 islands and 1,010 mainland regions were taken from Schrader et al.9 and then associated with islands for which we have bee species checklists. These data were originally sourced from the GIFT v.3.2 database using the R package GIFT86 and are taxonomically standardized according to the World Checklist of Vascular Plants9,20. In the few cases where we had bee checklist data for an island or archipelago that did not correspond to an island or archipelago in the GIFT database—for example, data aggregated at archipelago level in one but not the other—we calculated area and isolation directly from the aforementioned spatial map of islands63 and island-specific literature was used to determine island category and archipelago.

We incorporated additional island-level environmental information by overlaying our island shapefile with a spatial global shapefile of ecoregions62, which is an update of the original WWF biogeographical regionalization of Olson et al.87. This dataset provides a globally standardized classification of terrestrial ecoregions, biomes and biogeographic realms, and was selected because it offers consistent, GIS-based borders that explicitly include oceanic islands, allowing reproducible assignment of islands based solely on spatial overlap. Although developed as a general terrestrial biodiversity classification rather than for specific taxa, the underlying climatic, floristic and evolutionary discontinuities that define these realms are expected to also be relevant for bees, whose distributions are closely tied to vegetation structure and climatic regimes. Each island was assigned to a terrestrial biome and biogeographic realm using the intersect function from the R package sf (v1.0-2188). Biome classifications were aggregated into broader categories (boreal, desert, Mediterranean, temperate and tropical) for comparative purposes (Supplementary Table 13) and the final selected biome was the dominant biome found on the island. Realm classifications were one of Afrotropic, Australasia, Indomalaya, Nearctic, Neotropic, Oceania and Palaearctic. This allowed for consistent ecological context across islands and facilitated analyses of native bee richness by biome type and realm.

We also calculated additional isolation metrics by computing the edge-to-edge distance (km) from each study island to the nearest landmass across three size classes (>1 km2, >1,000 km2 and >10,000 km2) and the cumulative surrounding land area (km2) within buffers of 10 km, 100 km and 1,000 km around each island. To do this, we combined our global island database with a global continental layer from rnaturalearth v1.0.189. We tested correlations (r > 0.7) among all isolation variables prior to model fitting (Supplementary Fig. 1). We selected distance to the nearest landmass >1,000 km2 and the total land area within the 10 km buffer to represent isolation, alongside distance to mainland (km), in the final set of variables with which we conducted model selection. Climate data were extracted from bioclimatic rasters from the CHELSA v2.190 with a resolution of 30 arcsec. The variables included annual mean temperature (BIO1), temperature seasonality (BIO4; defined as the standard deviation of monthly mean temperatures multiplied by 100), annual precipitation (BIO12), and precipitation seasonality (BIO15; defined as the coefficient of variation of monthly precipitation). Local elevation metrics were extracted for each island using the elevatr package (v0.99.1)91. Climate variables were averaged for each island and elevation was recorded as the elevational range of each island.

It has been revealed that to ensure comparability and ecological and biogeographical relevance, we limited our final dataset to islands with a minimum area of 5 km2 and located at least 1 km from the mainland. These thresholds helped to remove islands with high edge effects, and limited habitat heterogeneity, while ensuring a meaningful biogeographical break from the mainland.

It has been revealed that to explore global patterns of bee sampling on islands we used the BeeBDC protocol outlined in Dorey et al.84 to extract all global records of bees on islands. Specifically, we downloaded all records of Anthophila from Global Biodiversity Information Facility92, Atlas of Living Australia93 and iDigBio. We corrected synonymous names as above using the synonym lists from Dorey et al.84 and Orr et al.4. As part of the cleaning process the data were subset to only include names of species found in the island checklist dataset, ensuring incorrect records of valid species unlikely to occur on the island were removed. To link bee occurrence records with islands spatially, we reprojected all coordinates to match the island shapefile and performed a spatial join, retaining only records intersecting island polygons defined in the checklist dataset. To ensure consistency between occurrence and checklist data, all species listed in the island checklists were added as supplementary records to the public database, standardizing species richness values across sources. The final dataset comprised 663,189 georeferenced records, which were subsequently used to assess sampling effort and spatial coverage across islands included in the analysis. This dataset was used to calculate a proxy for sampling effort and sampling completeness. To measure sampling completeness we calculated sampling coverage across islands using the Chao & Jost64 method via the coverage function in the iNEXT3D R package (v1.08)94. We used a species/island abundance (count of all occurrences per species per island) matrix of all records to estimate the proportion of the total individuals per island that belong to the observed species, using a non-parametric estimator that accounts for the frequency of rare species (singletons and doubletons). To account for large differences in sampling effort we additionally weighted coverage based on the total number of occurrence records, subsequently referred to as a sample-size-adjusted measure of sampling completeness.

We used the Discover Life global checklist through the BeeBDC tool84 as our baseline source for global bee species richness. To generate an estimate of mainland-only species richness, we excluded all species known to occur on islands by comparing with the above checklists and by removing all island-level records from the global checklist. The global checklist was also used to supplement endemism and island-only species data by filtering out species only recorded on islands from the checklist and cross-referencing with the island dataset. The mainland checklist was also used to test island occurrence patterns to create a binary classification of all species as either occurring or not occurring on islands.

According to recent reports, we used the island-level checklists to test the key predictors of species richness on islands. We fit a linear mixed-effects model using the lmer function from the lme4 R package (v1.1-37)95, with native species richness as the response variable. We log10-transformed native species richness after adding 1 to all values to accommodate islands with zero native bee species (n = 4) while preserving them in the analysis.

Sources indicate that we constructed a full model including the full set of ecological predictors, and then tested all possible model subsets (dredge function, R package MuMIn v1.48.1196). In all models, log10-transformed island area and a measure of island isolation were retained as fixed effects because these variables represent the core predictions of island biogeography theory. We evaluated three alternative isolation metrics in separate full models: log10-transformed distance to the nearest mainland, log10-transformed distance to the nearest landmass exceeding 1,000 km2, and the surrounding land area in a 10 km buffer around the island.

Recent findings suggest that the full model also included biome (5 categories), elevation range (log10), mean annual temperature (scaled), temperature seasonality (log10), annual precipitation (log10), precipitation seasonality (log10), island type (continental, fragment, or oceanic), and sampling completeness (sample-size-adjusted coverage, log10). We also evaluated an Area × Biome interaction and an Isolation × Biome interaction. We assessed collinearity among predictors using variance inflation factors (VIF; R package car, vif function97); mean annual temperature showed high collinearity with biome and other climate variables across all datasets (VIF > 5), and removing it from the full model brought all remaining predictors below this threshold. We therefore excluded mean annual temperature from the full model. Archipelago identity was included as a random intercept in all models to account for spatial non-independence among islands within the same archipelago and to allow baseline species richness to vary among archipelagos98. Models were fit by maximum likelihood and ranked by AICc; models with all three isolation-metric were then pooled into a single ranked set of models. When more than one model was within ΔAICc < 2, we selected the simplest model with the fewest degrees of freedom (Supplementary Table 4). The best-supported model included:.

log10(NativeSpeciesRichness)ij = β0 + β1 × log10(Area)ij + β2 × Biomeij + β3 × (log10(Area)ij × Biomeij) + β4 × log10(Isolation)ij + β5 × IslandTypeij + β6 × SamplingCompletenessij + uj + εij.

NativeSpeciesRichnessij = number of native bee species observed on island i in archipelago j.

Isolationij = distance to nearest mainland (km).

IslandTypeij = island type (continental, fragment, oceanic).

SamplingCompletenessij = sample-size-adjusted coverage.

β3 = interaction between log10(area) and biome.

β4 = effect of log10(isolation)β5 = effects of island type.

β6 = effect of sampling completeness.

uj = random intercept for archipelago j.

The final model included the interaction between area and biome, indicating that the effect of area on species richness varies among biomes. Island type and sampling completeness were retained as fixed effects. Two island groups for which coverage could not be calculated were dropped from the final model (Wallis and Futuna, Pitcairn Islands, n = 303). We quantified variance explained by fixed effects alone using marginal R2 and using conditional R2 for variance explained by both fixed and random effects99. To compare species–area relationship slopes among biomes, we extracted biome-specific slopes and their standard errors from the variance–covariance matrix of fixed effects. We then tested for specific differences among biomes using pairwise comparisons of estimated marginal means for intercepts and estimated marginal trends for slopes (FDR correction100) using the emmeans package (v1.11.1)101. Model predictions and confidence intervals were generated using the fixed-effects design matrix and visualized using ggplot2 (v3.5.2)102. Finally, we fit the same best model for only oceanic and only continental and fragment islands, specifically to compare ISAR slopes among biomes of different island types.

In a recent development, to explore the predictors of endemic species richness and its relationship with total species richness across islands, we used a model selection approach mirroring our richness analysis. We fit a series of linear mixed-effects models using the lmer function from the R package lme4 (v1.1-37)95. Collinearity among predictors was assessed the same way as for richness and mean annual temperature was also removed from all endemism full models.

In a recent development, we focused on islands supporting at least one single-island endemic (SIE ≥ 1; n = 113 islands). In this subset of islands, all biomes are represented apart from boreal, as the boreal islands harboured no endemics. We used the same model fitting procedure as described for the native richness analysis. All models within ΔAICc < 2 are shown in Supplementary Table 7. The best-supported model included:.

log10(Endemism)ij = β0 + β1 × log10(Area)ij + β2 × Biomeij + β3 × (log10(Area)ij × Biomeij) + β4 × log10(TemperatureSeasonality)ij + β5 × log10(Isolation)ij + uj + εij.

Endemismij = number of single-island endemic bee species observed on island i in archipelago j.

TemperatureSeasonalityij = temperature seasonality.

Isolationij = distance to nearest landmass >1,000 km2.

β3 = interaction between log10(area) and biome.

β4 = effect of log10(temperature seasonality).

β5 = effect of log10(isolation).

uj = random intercept for archipelago j.

To assess the generality of endemism patterns, we repeated analyses on three subsets: (1) oceanic islands only (n = 69), where endemism is more probably driven by neo-endemic evolution rather than the retention of land-bridge palaeo-endemics; (2) endemic-rich islands (SIE > 5% of total richness; n = 96), focusing on systems where endemism is well-established. We also repeated all analyses for AEs (species endemic to entire archipelagos; AE ≥ 1; n = 217) to confirm patterns were robust across endemism definitions (Supplementary Tables 5 and  7). The archipelago-level approach captures archipelago-wide diversification processes while revealing which individual islands within archipelagos are endemism hotspots (see, for example, ref. 48). For the SIE ≥ 1 and oceanic island subsets, the variance of the archipelago random effect was estimated at zero; however, it was kept for consistency across all models.

Additionally, to formally test how the relationship between richness and endemism varies across biomes, we compared three nested models for SIEs and AEs:.

where endemism is predicted solely by richness: log10(SIE/AE) ~ log10(Richness) + (1|Archipelago);.

where biome adds information beyond richness: log10(SIE/AE) ~ log10(Richness) + Biome + (1|Archipelago); and.

where the slope of the effect of richness varies by biome: log10(SIE/AE) ~ log10(Richness) × Biome + (1|Archipelago).

We compared these nested models sequentially using likelihood ratio tests. If including biome as a fixed effect significantly improves model fit, this indicates that islands with similar richness support different baseline levels of endemism depending on biome. If including the interaction between biome and richness improves model fit then the rate at which endemics accumulate with increasing richness also varies across biomes. We then tested for specific differences among biomes using pairwise comparisons of estimated marginal means for intercepts and estimated marginal trends for slopes (FDR correction100) using the emmeans package (V1.11.1)101.

Recent findings suggest that to assess the extent to which bee diversity tracks angiosperm diversity across islands, we fitted a linear regression model with native bee richness as the response variable and native angiosperm richness and its interaction with biome as the predictors. We additionally included both island area and isolation as covariates to account for confounding geographic effects that influence the richness of both angiosperms and bees. Variance inflation factors indicated low multicollinearity among predictors (all VIFs < 2.4), supporting the inclusion of angiosperm richness, island area, and isolation in the same model. We fit the model for the 175 islands for which we had both bee native richness data and reliable angiosperm richness data from the GIFT database20. Archipelago identity was included as a random intercept to account for spatial non-independence of islands within the same archipelago. To include the interaction with biome we removed boreal islands from the analysis as there were too few islands (3) with which to test the interaction.

Sources indicate that to (1) compare baseline shifts (intercepts) across biomes against a single baseline and (2) to conduct a likelihood ratio test on the significance of the interaction between biome and angiosperm richness, we additionally fitted a model with and without the angiosperm richness × biome interaction term. The full model with interaction was:.

log10(NativeSpeciesRichness)ij = β0 + β1 × log10(AngiospermRichness)ij + β2 × Biomeij + β3 × (log10(AngiospermRichness)ij × Biomeij) + β4 × log10(Area)ij + β5 × log10(Isolation)ij + uj + εij.

NativeSpeciesRichnessij = native bee species richness on island i in archipealgo j.

AngiospermRichnessij = native angiosperm species richness.

Isolationij = distance to nearest mainland (km).

β1 = effect of log10(angiosperm richness).

β3 = interaction between log10(angiosperm richness) and biome.

β5 = effect of log10(isolation).

uj = random intercept for archipelago j.

In a recent development, using the coefficients from this model, we computed an adjusted bee richness for each island by subtracting the centred contributions of angiosperm richness, island area, and isolation from the observed values. This adjustment standardizes the data, showing the bee richness for each island if it had the global average plant richness, land area, and isolation. Finally, we calculated estimated marginal means for each biome using the emmeans package (V1.11.1)101, and performed post hoc pairwise comparisons (FDR correction)100.

All statistical analyses, data manipulation, and visualizations were conducted in R (v4.5.0)103. In addition to the packages already cited; data processing, post hoc tests, and figure formatting were carried out using the following packages: broom.mixed (v0.2.9.6)104, ComplexUpset (v1.3.3)105, corrplot (v0.95)106, cowplot (v1.2.0)107, ggnewscale (v0.5.1)108, ggrepel (v0.9.6)109, ggtext (v0.1.2)110, kableExtra (v1.4.0)111, lmerTest (v3.1-3)112, maps (v3.4.2.1)113, mgcv (v1.9-4)114, multcomp (v1.4-28)115, multcompView (v0.1−10)116, patchwork (v1.3.0)117, performance (v0.13.0)118, scales (v1.4.0)119, scico (v1.5.0)120, tidyverse (v2.0.0)121 and UpSetR (v1.4.1)122.

In a recent development, (A) Biome-specific island species–area relationships. Solid lines represent fitted mean regression lines from mixed-effects model, with dashed lines indicating 95% confidence intervals. Slopes (β) are reported for each biome. Point colour indicates the proportion of endemic species per island. Labelled islands are the top 10% most species-rich islands within each biome (values in parentheses show total native bee richness). (B) Relationship between island isolation (log10 distance to mainland) and native bee species richness. Solid line represents fitted mean regression line from mixed-effects model, with dashed lines indicating 95% confidence intervals. The effect of isolation was evaluated using a two-sided t-test with Satterthwaite’s approximation (β = −0.15, 95% CI = [−0.26, −0.03], t(130.5) = −2.56, p = 0.012). Point colour indicates the proportion of endemic species per island.

Recent findings suggest that (A) Biome-specific island species–area relationships. Solid lines represent fitted mean regression lines from mixed-effects model, with dashed lines indicating 95% confidence intervals. Slopes (β) are reported for each biome. Point colour indicates the proportion of endemic species per island. Labelled islands are the top 10% most species-rich islands within each biome (values in parentheses show total native bee richness). (B) Relationship between island isolation (log10 distance to mainland) and native bee species richness. Solid line represents fitted mean regression line from mixed-effects model, with dashed lines indicating 95% confidence intervals. The effect of isolation was evaluated using a two-sided t-test with Satterthwaite’s approximation (β = −0.05, 95% CI = [−0.18, 0.08], t(75.7) = 0.72, p = 0.475). Point colour indicates the proportion of endemic species per island.

Solid lines represent fitted mean regression lines from mixed-effects model, with dashed lines indicating 95% confidence intervals. Point colour indicates the proportion of endemic species per island. Sampling completeness is represented by the log10-transformed sample-size-adjusted coverage on each island. The effect of sampling completeness was evaluated using a two-sided t-test with Satterthwaite’s approximation (β = 0.22, 95% CI = [0.13,0.31], t(294.5) = 4.73, p = 3.46 × 10−6). n = 303 islands.

Sources indicate that (A) Relationship between island area (log10 km2) and single-island endemic (SIE) species richness for oceanic islands with at least one single-island endemic (n = 69 islands). Solid black line represents fitted mean regression line from mixed-effects model, with dashed lines indicating 95% confidence intervals. The effect of area was evaluated using a two-sided t-test with Satterthwaite’s approximation (β = 0.32, 95% CI = [0.22, 0.42], t(69) = 6.23, p = 3.18 × 10−8). Circles are coloured by the proportion of native species that are endemic. (B) Relationship between island isolation (log10 distance to nearest mainland, km) and SIE richness for oceanic islands. Black line and confidence interval, and circle colours as in panel A. The effect of isolation was evaluated using a two-sided t-test with Satterthwaite’s approximation (β = −0.05, 95% CI = [−0.17, 0.06], t(69) = −0.92, p = 0.36). (C) Relationship between island area (log10 km2) and single-island endemic (SIE) species richness for islands where endemics comprise more than 5% of native bee richness (n = 96 islands). Black line and confidence interval, and circle colours as in panel A. The effect of area was evaluated using a two-sided t-test with Satterthwaite’s approximation (β = 0.36, 95% CI = [0.30, 0.43], t(69.8) = 10.74, p = 2 × 10−16). Circles are coloured by the proportion of native species that are endemic. (D) Relationship between island isolation (log10 distance to nearest mainland, km) and SIE richness for endemic-rich islands. Black line and confidence interval, and circle colours as in panel A. The effect of isolation was evaluated using a two-sided t-test with Satterthwaite’s approximation (β = −0.07, 95% CI = [−0.20, 0.06], t(75.8) = −1.06, p = 0.29). Circles are coloured by the proportion of native species that are endemic.

(A) Single-island endemics (n = 113 islands). (B) Archipelago endemics species that are archipelago endemics across biomes (n = 217 islands). Violins show the kernel density distribution of the data. Overlaid box plots represent the median (center line) and 25th and 75th percentiles (bounds of box /interquartile range (IQR)); whiskers extend to the minimum and maximum values within 1.5×IQR.

Industry observers note that (A) Relationship between island area (log10 km2) and archipelago endemic (AE) species richness, for islands with at least one archipelago endemic. Solid lines represent fitted mean regression lines from mixed-effects model, with dashed lines indicating 95% confidence intervals. Circles are coloured by the proportion of native species that are endemic at the archipelago level. Labelled islands are the top 10% highest in AE richness with the number of AEs in parentheses. (B) Relationship between isolation (log10 km from mainland) and AE richness. Solid line represents fitted mean regression line from mixed-effects model, with dashed lines indicating 95% confidence intervals. The effect of isolation was evaluated using a two-sided t-test with Satterthwaite’s approximation (β = −0.04, 95% CI = [−0.17,], t(173) = −0.71, p = 0.48). Circle colour as in panel A. (C) Relationship between elevation range (log10 m) and AE richness. The effect of elevation range was evaluated using a two-sided t-test with Satterthwaite’s approximation (β = 0.18, 95% CI = [0.04, 0.33], t(216.6) = 2.51, p = 0.01). Black line and confidence interval, and circle colours as in panel B. (D) Relationship between sampling completeness (log10 sample-size-adjusted coverage) and AE richness. The effect of sampling completeness was evaluated using a two-sided t-test with Satterthwaite’s approximation (β = 0.13, 95% CI = [0.03, 0.24], t(216.8) = 2.50, p = 0.01). Black line and confidence interval, and circle colours as in panel B.

(A) Relationship between total native species richness (log10) and single-island endemic (SIE) richness (log10), coloured by biome. Including biome significantly improved model fit (two-sided likelihood ratio test; χ² = 33.18, df = 3, p = 2.95 × 10−7) Table S7); letters denote groups that differ significantly based on two-sided post-hoc pairwise comparisons of estimated marginal means (FDR correction, p < 0.05). Overlaid box plots represent the median (center line) and 25th and 75th percentiles (bounds of box/interquartile range (IQR)); whiskers extend to the minimum and maximum values within 1.5×IQR. (C) Relationship between total native species richness (log10) and archipelago endemics (AE; islands with at least one AE, n = 217 islands) richness (log10), coloured by biome. Solid lines represent fitted mean regression lines from mixed-effects model, with dashed lines indicating 95% confidence intervals. (D) Residuals from the AE richness model across biomes (n = 217). Boxplots, violins and letters are the same as in Panel B. Including biome significantly improved model fit (two-sided likelihood ratio test, χ2 = 40.37, df = 3, p = 8.90 × 10−9; Table S7).

David Moyes credited Everton with giving him his first big break in management as he prepares to oversee a record-breaking 593rd match in charge of the club.

Moyes is set to surpass Harry Catterick's record of 592 games managed as Everton boss when his side make the trip to face Brentford in the Premier League.

He first made the move to Merseyside in 2002 from Preston North End and remained in the Everton dugout for 11 years before replacing Alex Ferguson at Manchester United.

The 63-year-old went on to have spells at Real Sociedad, Sunderland and West Ham before returning to Everton in January 2025 to replace Sean Dyche.

During his two stints with the Toffees, Moyes has overseen 250 wins in all competitions (D155 L187), and his Everton side have started the 2026-27 campaign brightly.

Everton are seventh after signing off for the international break with a win over Coventry City, and Moyes wants that upward trajectory to continue in his milestone match.

"I'm really thrilled about it, but if I'm honest, it's not something I really think about," Moyes told reporters ahead of the trip to the Gtech Community Stadium.

"I've suddenly become the manager who has managed more Everton games than anyone before. That's a privilege and an honour to be put in that position.

"I have to thank the people who brought me to the club. When you take a chance on a young manager, you never know if it'll work, but they had faith and believed in me.

"I'm so thankful for the people around Everton because they've been so good for me.".

Andrews' side have, however, won four of their last seven Premier League games at the Gtech (D2 L1), and are looking for back-to-back home league wins for the first time in 2026, having last done so in November 2025 (three in a row).

But the Bees have won just one of their last 11 Premier League games that have come the matchday following an international break (D5 L5) – although that was the only such match they played on a Monday in this period, beating West Ham 2-0 in October 2025.

Everton, meanwhile, have lost just one of their last eight Premier League games against Brentford (W3 D4), though they are winless in their last four against them (D3 L1).

According to recent reports, this will be Everton's ninth top-flight game played on a Monday since the start of last season, three more than any other side in this time (Manchester United six). The Toffees have lost just one of their last seven on this day of the week (W2 D4), winning their last two away from home.

Moyes' men have won back-to-back Premier League games for the first time since between February and March, and are looking to win three in a row in the competition for the first time since May 2025.

By Saikat Mandal | 21 Nov 2026 15:08.

Two of the Premier League's most successful clubs renew their fierce rivalry on Sunday as Liverpool welcome Manchester United to Anfield for their first meeting of the season.

The Reds are navigating a period of transition under Andoni Iraola, but have made an encouraging start to the campaign, climbing to fourth in the Premier League table with 18 points.

Manchester United, meanwhile, have endured their worst start to a new season, prompting the club hierarchy to part ways with Michael Carrick, who guided them into the Champions League places last term.

The Red Devils have wasted little time in appointing Mauricio Pochettino as his successor, but the Argentine faces a daunting introduction to the rivalry, having won just three of his 19 managerial meetings with Liverpool.

Here, Sports Mole provides everything you need to know about how to tune into the contest.

Liverpool vs Man Utd is one of two Premier League fixtures scheduled for Sunday, with the other seeing Hull City welcome Brighton & Hove Albion.

The eagerly anticipated clash at Anfield is scheduled to get underway at 4.30pm UK time, a prime Sunday afternoon slot that should allow supporters both in the stands and watching from around the world to savour one of English football's biggest rivalries.

Liverpool vs Man Utd will take place at Anfield, the 61,276-capacity stadium that has served as the spiritual home of the mighty Reds since 1892.

Anfield is the fifth-largest football stadium in England and has been the setting for countless memorable encounters between these fierce rivals, with its famous atmosphere often adding another layer of intensity.

Beyond football, the iconic venue also opens its doors to major musical events during the off-season, with global superstar Taylor Swift among the significant-name artists to have performed there during her record-breaking Eras Tour.

Non-Sky customers can stream the contest through a NOW Day or cancel-anytime Month pass, while viewers in India can catch the action live on JioHotstar.

Liverpool and Man Utd's official X accounts are expected to share match snippets throughout the contest, while journalists covering the game may also post their own footage and updates.

After the final whistle, extended highlights should be available on both clubs' official YouTube channels, while viewers in the UK can catch the action again on BBC's Match of the Day 2.

Liverpool have an opportunity to cut the gap to Manchester City to just one point with victory on Sunday, giving them an added incentive to make home advantage count.

The Reds have endured an uncomfortable run against their fiercest rivals at Anfield, having failed to beat the Red Devils on home soil since their emphatic 7-0 triumph in March 2023, and Iraola will be desperate to put that unwanted sequence behind them by claiming all three points.

The likes of Bradley Barcola and Florian Wirtz will be eager to rise to the occasion and deliver on a stage of such magnitude, but Liverpool's overriding priority is to turn their home performances into consistent results and strengthen their position in the title race.

For Man Utd, the stakes are arguably even higher, with the visitors desperate to climb out of the relegation zone and give their troubled campaign some much-needed impetus.

Pochettino, meanwhile, will be keen to mark the beginning of his Man Utd tenure with a statement victory, although he could hardly have been handed a more demanding opening assignment; given the circumstances, even a hard-earned draw at Anfield would represent a respectable start to his reign.

Published: 18:00 EST, 20 November 2026 | Updated: 18:06 EST, 20 November 2026.

Tottenham star Tosin Adarabioyo has joined forces with former Chelsea team-mates Reece James and Levi Colwill to launch a trading card shop in London.

Card Cop, opening in Borough Market on Thursday, will sell cards from a variety of sports as well as other collections such as Pokemon and Marvel.

It has been revealed that adarabioyo began collecting as a child and returned to the hobby in 2020. His collection, which he shares on social media, spans a variety of sports and he also has several of Brazilian icon Neymar.

'I’ve been collecting for years, and it’s great to see the hobby continue to grow,' said the 29-year-old, who left Chelsea for Spurs last summer.

'I love collecting. It’s a great way for supporters to connect with their favourite players. I’ve always felt that collectors are some of the most passionate fans.

'I’ve got to know so many collectors through the hobby. Talking about our collections is an instant icebreaker, and I know those conversations can mean a lot. I want to bring more players into the hobby and recreate those moments.

Tosin Adarabioyo, like many footballers, has a passion for collecting trading cards.

The newly introduced shop is set to open in London's Borough Market next week.

Adarabioyo enjoyes collecting cards of former PSG star Neymar, who won 130 caps for Brazil.

'Neymar is criminally underrated to me, and I think his cards are too. Some of the images take me straight back to performances I’ve watched over the years. It’s hard to describe, but it’s like bottling up that feeling forever. Football purists will know what I mean.'.

West Ham defender Kyle Walker-Peters, who played with Tosin at England youth level, is among backers along with James and Colwill.

Adarabioyo already has an online retail business, The Huddle, with guests such as Dominic Solanke, Robert Sanchez and Adam Wharton all featuring on live streams, opening boxes as fans watch.

Recent figures valued the global sports trading card market at $13.75billion (£10.5bn) in 2025, with that projected to grow to $27.52bn (£21bn) by 2034.

Formula One star Lewis Hamilton got in on the act earlier this year, launching his own venture and a shop in Frankfurt.

The seven-time world champion was already an ambassador for Topps - who also have the licence for Premier League cards - and mentioned: 'I’ve loved collecting cards since I was a kid — Pokemon, football, anything I could get my hands on.

Industry observers note that 'To now play a role in shaping the future of the category is incredible. We have a significant opportunity to tap into the culture in a way no one has before.'.

By Ben Knapton | 21 Nov 2026 15:24, Last updated: 21 Nov 2026 15:43.

Chelsea have been dealt yet another injury blow concerning Moises Caicedo, who was forced off in the first half of Saturday's Premier League clash with Leeds United.

The 25-year-old was making his sixth start of the top-flight season at Stamford Bridge, joining Romeo Lavia in the centre of the park, but his race was run with just 22 minutes gone.

Caicedo was involved in a heavy mid-air collision with James Justin early doors and was left in a heap on the ground, but he was ultimately able to carry on, albeit briefly.

The Ecuador international sat down on the turf just moments later and covered his face with his arm as he was attended to by medical staff, before hobbling off the field to be replaced by Jordan Henderson.

Caicedo appeared to be struggling with a back injury and was given an ice pack as he sat down on the bench, shortly before the Blues took the lead through Emmanuel Emegha.

The severity of Caicedo's latest concern is yet to be ascertained, and it may well be that the South American simply sustained a contact injury which will heal in a matter of days.

However, the midfielder's withdrawal prolonged a painful stop-start season, in which he has already missed six games across the Premier League and EFL Cup due to two separate injuries.

Caicedo sat out Chelsea's opening two games vs. Fulham and Luton Town owing to a knock, before picking up a calf problem just 14 minutes into his first appearance of the campaign against Brighton & Hove Albion.

The Blues faced Leeds (in the EFL Cup), Arsenal, Hull City and Brentford without Caicedo due to his new calf problem, since when he has been a mainstay in Alonso's midfield with the captain's armband.

The Ecuadorian is now an early doubt for next Friday's trip to Nottingham Forest, though, as well as Chelsea's London derby at home to Crystal Palace on December 2.

Caicedo's fitness struggles in the 2026-27 season are uncharacteristic, as the 25-year-old missed just two games through injury or illness in his first three campaigns at the club.

Both of those absences occurred in his debut 2023-24 campaign, in which he missed a 0-0 draw with Bournemouth because of a knock, and a 2-1 defeat to Wolverhampton Wanderers due to illness.

Caicedo navigated the entire 2024-25 season without picking up an injury, starting all 38 Premier League games and being omitted from several Conference League squads to enjoy a well-earned rest.

The midfielder then made another 50 appearances in the 2025-26 season, and his only notable absences were due to suspension rather than fitness problems.

Alonso is already missing Joao Pedro, Jamie Gittens, Maxence Lacroix, Jorrel Hato and Reece James, and none is expected to return before the end of the month.

Are you keeping track of your players so they don’t stay up late at night playing GTA?

“I will let my friend Gennaro Gattuso respond. Jokes aside, I don’t care.”.

Is a winner a dreamer who never gives up? Are you a dreamer?

LA communities kick out Significant Oil

📅 02 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1060 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dw

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Los Angeles has become the largest city in the US to ban oil drilling, after years of lawsuits and campaigning by residents who raised the alarm over pollution and potential health risks from nearby wells .
  • "Front-line communities have pushed the city for a solution for this for over a decade," mentioned local resident Wendy Miranda, who has campaigned for years with STAND-LA, a coalition of community groups working to end neighborhood oil drilling.
  • The ordinance, approved by the LA City Council on October 28, puts an immediate stop to oil extraction and bans the redrilling or deepening of wells.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Los Angeles has become the largest city in the US to ban oil drilling, after years of lawsuits and campaigning by residents who raised the alarm over pollution and potential health risks from nearby wells .

"Front-line communities have pushed the city for a solution for this for over a decade," mentioned local resident Wendy Miranda, who has campaigned for years with STAND-LA, a coalition of community groups working to end neighborhood oil drilling.

The ordinance, approved by the LA City Council on October 28, puts an immediate stop to oil extraction and bans the redrilling or deepening of wells. Existing operations must be phased out within city limits over the next 20 years.

Though LA City is only part of greater Los Angeles, the move affects hundreds of active wells and thousands of inactive ones, many located in working class communities of color.

Sources indicate that "In South LA, working-class families have had corporations drilling across the street from their homes," noted council president Marqueece Harris-Dawson in a statement. "No one should have to live near an oil drilling site.".

Rock Zierman, CEO of the California Independent Petroleum Association (CIPA), told DW, "CIPA believes this ordinance constitutes an unlawful taking of private property.".

LA follows much smaller Culver City, also in California, in moving against urban oil production, and begins the process of ending its long, complex relationship with fossil fuels.

In a recent development, california's oil industry expanded rapidly in the early 20th century, when the state produced roughly a quarter of the world's oil. Lots of that so-called black gold was around LA and as the city grew, homes, schools and businesses were built around existing oil infrastructure.

Today, wells can be found beneath residential areas, close to playgrounds, along the coast and in some of the city's most densely populated and largely working-class neighborhoods. Some have been permanently sealed or plugged for decades, while others remain active or are idle.

Under California law, an idle well is one that has not produced oil for two years. Unlike plugged wells, they can potentially return to production.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

Recent findings suggest that residents living near the active and inactive wells report strong odors, headaches, nausea and breathing difficulties. Another concern is air quality. Oil wells can release toxic pollutants, including benzene and hydrogen sulfide, and research has linked proximity to oil extraction with higher rates of respiratory illness and reduced lung function.

But both active and idle wells can also leak methane — a potent greenhouse gas that contributes to climate change — while residents say occasional accidents or breakages send oil flowing down city streets.

"Frontline communities have been experiencing or have experienced for decades living near these toxic sites and having to pay for that with their health," said Miranda, a policy director with Esperanza Community Housing, a nonprofit providing affordable housing services.

It has been revealed that miranda told DW she and her mother both have asthma. The council vote "definitely represents hope," she added.

Industry observers note that LA City Council initially approved an ordinance to phase out oil extraction back in 2022 after successful lobbying by residents like Wendy Miranda. But oil companies challenged the measure in court, with industry groups successfully arguing that the city lacked the legal authority to impose the ban.

California subsequently passed legislation giving local governments greater power to regulate and restrict oil and gas operations, putting the possibility of a phaseout back on the table.

In an emailed statement to DW, CIPA CEO Rock Zierman remarked energy companies were prepared to challenge the new ordinance.

Zierman added that it would make city residents more dependent on foreign oil from countries with lower environmental standards when they are "already struggling" with high gas prices.

"It sends the jobs, investment and revenue elsewhere while leaving Californians to pay the bill," noted Zierman.

According to recent reports, the relationship between local oil production and prices at the pump is not straightforward and is influenced by a number of factors, according to the California Energy Commission, the state's main energy policy agency. Those include the cost of crude oil, refining, transportation, distribution and local taxes.

Even though the US is the world's largest oil producer, it exports and imports crude oil, as well as refined petroleum products. Because oil is traded globally, US residents are exposed to the same price fluctuations as people elsewhere, no matter how much of the fossil fuel is produced domestically.

California's oil industry and the amount of oil it produces have been steadily declining since the 1980s. In the coastal lowlands known as the LA Basin, output is 43% lower than eight years ago, with the amount of oil extracted falling more rapidly than the number of open wells.

When wells stop producing, it is up to the oil operators to remove equipment and plug them. The state agency that regulates oil and gas, CalGEM, and the LA fire department oversee plugging operations, and also seal wells for which no-one takes responsibility.

But many have not yet been plugged — some 80% of idle wells in LA have been inactive for more than eight years, and about a third for over a century.

According to recent reports, the cost of plugging a well also varies widely, with estimates ranging from hundreds of thousands to millions of dollars. California law requires operators to submit plugging plans or face annual fines that increase with the amount of time the well has been idle.

It has been revealed that but those fines aren't always paid. According to CalGEM's own data, the agency collected just $1 million out of $36 million (€32 million) in fines in 2025.

A report by Carbon Tracker also found that if all future profits from oil companies operating in California went to decommissioning wells, the state would still face a shortfall of $7 billion. The cost would by default fall to taxpayers, according to Carbon Tracker.

Miranda told DW that the next step for community activists is to reduce the 20-year timeline and have the oil sector "pay for this cleanup."  For now, she is says both she and her mother are hopeful that future generations "can have better health and breathe cleaner air.".

City have failed to win a WSL home game under Jeglertz for the first time, ending the second-longest winning streak on home turf in the competition (17 in a row).

Despite the loss, Jeglertz is not too concerned about the result as he feels he will get a strong response from his side.

#60509. Ice hockey officials considering options after CAS order to reinstate Russia

Ice hockey officials considering options after CAS order to reinstate Russia

📅 02 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (961 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dw

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The president of the International Ice Hockey Federation (IIHF), Franz Reindl, confirmed shortly after the decision by the Court of Arbitration for Sport (CAS) on Friday, that he had called a meeting of its main decision-making body for Monday and Tuesday.
  • The Lausanne-based court had ruled that the IIHF must allow Russian national teams to take part in ice hockey world championships again.
  • "Our task now is to implement this ruling responsibly," remarked Germany's Reindl, who was elected IIHF president just last month.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The president of the International Ice Hockey Federation (IIHF), Franz Reindl, confirmed shortly after the decision by the Court of Arbitration for Sport (CAS) on Friday, that he had called a meeting of its main decision-making body for Monday and Tuesday.

The Lausanne-based court had ruled that the IIHF must allow Russian national teams to take part in ice hockey world championships again. They had been barred from doing so since shortly after Russia introduced its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022.

"Our task now is to implement this ruling responsibly," remarked Germany's Reindl, who was elected IIHF president just last month.

According to recent reports, "Several championships are only weeks away, and changes to participation affect many people; players, teams, organizing committees and host cities," he said. "We will work closely with all of them to find practical solutions.".

In a recent development, the first tournament the CAS decision applies to is the World Juniors, to be held beginning on December 26 in Canada. Just how it will affect the tournament is not clear. Hockey Canada said it was in contact with the IIHF and had briefed Prime Minister Mark Carney's government on the decision.

Foreign Affairs Minister Anita Anand told public broadcaster CBC that she is "not comfortable" with allowing a Russian team to take part in the tournament in Alberta.

"This is a very unwelcome decision given the geopolitical situation, given the actions of Russia," she said. "All options are on the table, and I will say, again, I greet this decision with great disappointment.".

Canada's secretary of state for sport, Adam van Koeverden, appeared to rule out Russian athletes being granted visas for the tournament.

"Canada will maintain restrictions on the participation of Russian athletes at events hosted in Canada that receive funding from the Government of Canada and explore further options to ensure that the Russian government is held accountable," he mentioned in a statement.

Germany is also considering its options as it prepares to host the Men's Ice Hockey World Championship in Gelsenkirchen, Düsseldorf and Mannheim in May.

"The German government takes a very critical view of the decision by the Court of Arbitration for Sport, a government spokesman stated on Sunday, according to the DPA news agency.

"The German government will discuss possible consequences of the ruling, including for the 2027 Ice Hockey World Championship in Germany, with the German Ice Hockey Federation (DEB) promptly.".

The DEB's chief executive, Frank Lutz, is to travel to Berlin to discuss the matter with government officials this week. Speaking on broadcaster MagentaSport on the weekend, he conceded that surrendering Germany's hosting rights for the lucrative tournament was a possibility.

"I do not want to paint a black picture. I do not want to call the World Championship into question either. But of course, we at the DEB also have to consider the option of handing back this championship," he noted.

Several other national ice hockey federations have expressed disappointment at the CAS decision, including those of Ukraine, Sweden, Finland, and Czechia.

In a recent development, the International Olympic Committee opened the door for Russian athletes to return to international competition when it lifted its ban of the Russian Olympic Committee in July. However, the IIHF had already decided to continue to exclude Russian teams for the 2026-27 season – over security concerns. The CAS decision – handed down after an appeal by Russia – found this reasoning was insufficiently proven.

The Kremlin's reaction to the ruling was, unsurprisingly, positive.

"Russia is returning to world hockey. This place rightfully belongs to us, and discrimination in hockey has been brought to an end," Sports Minister Mikhail Degtyarev told state television channel Vesti.

A boycott of the World Juniors, Men's World Championships or other tournaments by individual nations is now emerging as a real possibility.

"We are currently working to bring as many countries as possible into a united front to tell the IIHF that none of us will play against Russia under these circumstances," Finnish Ice Hockey Association boss Heikki Hietanen mentioned in a statement released on the organization's website on Monday evening.

"Our stance is that we will not play against Russia as long as the war of aggression against Ukraine continues," added Hietanen, who is also a member of the IIHF Council.

By Tuesday afternoon, the Finland-led effort was gaining steam, with Sweden, Norway and Denmark making similar statements.

"The Three Crowns will not play Russia in coming world championship tournaments," Swedish Ice Hockey Federation boss Anders Larsson noted in a statement.

This came shortly after Norway said it would not play Russia at the Men's World Championship and the Danish Ice Hockey Federation issued a similar statement on its website.

Industry observers note that "Denmark will – based on the current situation and the information available to us today – not play against Russia at the World Championship in Germany in May 2027," it read. Denmark did not qualify for the World Juniors tournament.

There has been the suggestion, that having won this victory at the CAS, Russia's next focus could be on football, where its national and club teams remain excluded from international competitions.

Russian FA general secretary Maxim Mitrofanov told state news agency Tass that there "should be one rule for all.".

World football's governing body FIFA allowed a Russia boys' team to play under its national flag in the inaugural Under-15 World Cup and Festival in Azerbaijan, which kicked off last week and ends on Saturday.

In a recent development, this article was originally published on November 2, 2026. It was updated on November 3 with the statement from the Finnish Ice Hockey Association. It was later updated with the statements from the Swedish, Norwegian and Danish federations.

The Manchester City loanee was punished by the club for failing to report to training sessions and missed several matches. He has not featured for four games: one because of illness, then a ‘breach of club discipline’ and a lack of fitness thereafter.

But Grealish will be considered for the squad when the in-form Toffees travel to Brentford on Monday night.

Moyes said: ‘He has served his punishment and we will treat him as we were treating him before.

It has been revealed that ‘We will get on with things. The team is going really well at the moment and what I don’t want to do is turn it into a Jack story because it shouldn’t be.’.

Pushed if that suggests he will not play on Monday night, Moyes replied: ‘He could easily. He is back in the squad, he is a good player. Who knows?’.

Jack Grealish is available for Everton again after serving his punishment and regaining fitness.

Everton have won their last three games and go into Monday’s match sixth in the table.

According to recent reports, asked what Grealish can offer, the boss added: ‘Jack can offer us a lot. I want more from him, I want him to show more than he has done. I want him to give me more assists, goals.

In a recent development, ‘But there's lots of things about him which we need and he's good at retaining the ball, giving us good possession, carrying. So we hope that he can get back to those levels and give us what we need.

‘I think this time last year he was probably sitting on five or six assists so we're hoping to get that.’.

Grealish's social media apology came after he featured in a behind-closed-doors match during the international break.

'Nice to be back out there with the boys today after a few good days training!' Grealish wrote. 'I want to apologise to the fans (and) everyone at the club for not being able to help the team the last few weeks.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • Tottenham Hotspur youngster Luca Williams-Barnett repaid Roberto De Zerbi's faith in him with a goal and assist in Saturday's 2-0 Premier League victory over Ipswich Town.
  • The 18-year-old was handed his first Premier League start against the Tractor Boys in place of the injured Mathys Tel, having shown glimpses of his potential off the bench against Leeds United and Crystal Palace.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

By Ben Knapton | 21 Nov 2026 17:00, Last updated: 21 Nov 2026 17:08.

Tottenham Hotspur youngster Luca Williams-Barnett repaid Roberto De Zerbi's faith in him with a goal and assist in Saturday's 2-0 Premier League victory over Ipswich Town.

The 18-year-old was handed his first Premier League start against the Tractor Boys in place of the injured Mathys Tel, having shown glimpses of his potential off the bench against Leeds United and Crystal Palace.

With 15 minutes gone at the Tottenham Hotspur Stadium, Williams-Barnett muscled his way beyond Abdoul Ouattara to meet Pedro Porro's cross and bundle the ball into the back of the net for the opening goal.

The 2008-born youngster followed up his maiden Premier League goal with a fine assist in the second period, driving down the left-hand side and crossing for Dominic Solanke to crash home.

Williams-Barnett made way for Savio in the 64th minute, having been booked shortly after Solanke's goal, but not without becoming Tottenham's third-youngest Premier League scorer ever.

At 18 years, one month and 20 days old, Williams-Barnett is only older than Andy Turner and Gareth Bale when they scored their first Premier League goals for Tottenham.

Turner holds the club record, having scored at just 17 years and five months against Everton in 1992, while Bale was just four days younger than Williams-Barnett is now when he netted against Fulham in September 2007.

Furthermore, Williams-Barnett has overtaken Tottenham traitor Sol Campbell on the list, as the latter was 18 years and two months old when he scored his maiden Spurs Premier League goal.

Aaron Lennon, Reto Ziegler and Dele Alli are the only other players in the top 10 to have scored their first Tottenham Premier League goals in the 2000s.

While Williams-Barnett stole the spotlight at the Tottenham Hotspur Stadium, the teenager did not quite manage to break either a club or Premier League record.

Despite both scoring and setting up a goal in North London, Williams-Barnett is only the second-youngest player to both score and assist in a Premier League game, behind Michael Owen.

The former Ballon d'Or winner was just 17 years and 364 days old when he scored and assisted for Liverpool against Crystal Palace in 1997, before also doing so against Leeds United at 18 years and 12 days.

Nevertheless, Williams-Barnett has made his case to also start next Sunday's clash away to Sunderland, as well as the first North London derby of the season on December 6.

Spurs' victory over Ipswich has lifted De Zerbi's side up to ninth in the Premier League table on 15 points from 11 matches, just three points worse off than fourth-placed Bournemouth.

Breaking: An inspiral of a star inside a common envelope with its giant companion

📅 22 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 41 min read (8167 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Nature

⏱️ ~41 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, the formation of compact stellar binaries requires rapid orbital tightening of their progenitor binary stars1,2.
  • This is a preview of subscription content, access via your institution.
  • Access Nature and 54 other Nature Portfolio journals.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, the formation of compact stellar binaries requires rapid orbital tightening of their progenitor binary stars1,2. This is theorized to happen through common envelope evolution (CEE)3, when the stars orbit in a loosely bound, shared convective envelope, triggering an inspiral due to frictional drag4,5. However, this inspiral in such a system has never been observed directly. Here we present observations of AT 2025abao, a transient eruption in the Andromeda Galaxy, which originates from the CEE of an approximately 7M⊙ asymptotic giant branch (AGB) star with its companion. Extensive pre- and post-eruption spectroscopy is best explained as an approximately 0.7M⊙ companion inspiralling within the convective AGB envelope that powers a seven-year period of gradual brighteningone of the first direct observations of frictional drag energy dissipation induced by CEE. This phase is radiatively efficient, consistent with predictions for convective transport in CEE5,6,7,8. The subsequent merger of the companion with the primary core powers the ejection of the outermost 10% of the stellar envelope at speeds about 10× the primary escape speed, and empirically constrains the fraction of dissipated orbital energy available to unbind the convective common envelope4,9,10,11, 0.01 ≲ α ≲ 0.4. This end-to-end characterization using multi-survey observations demonstrates a path towards mapping the landscape of CEE outcomes with upcoming surveys.

Optical spectra of the AT 2025abao eruption. Its spectral evolution matches the characteristic evolution seen in LRNe — blue continuum with emission lines at early times that transitions to a red continuum with molecular absorption features at late times.

Near-infrared spectra of AT 2025abao, from its precursor phase (red) and the eruption (blue). The spectra during the precursor phase resemble late M-type stars, while those during the eruption demonstrates a transition to hotter temperatures. Notably, the CO absorption bands are seen in all spectra, indicating that some molecular gas remains intact even after the eruption.

It has been revealed that theoretically calculated dust mass around the quiescent progenitor system as a function of binary mass ratio using analytical prescriptions (black line) and detailed simulations (squares). The black shaded region marks the range expected by varying stellar parameters in the analytical model (section ‘Comparisons to theoretical predictions of enhanced mass loss’). The observed dust mass from the archival progenitor SED and the JWST observation is shown in purple, which constrains the system mass ratio to \(q=0.1{0}_{-0.08}^{+0.10}\).

Previously identified sources such as V1309Sco, M31-LRN-2015, AT 2019zhd (circles) exhibit a gradual brightening by several magnitudes prior to its eruption. AT 2025abao (stars) differs from these sources, as it only demonstrates a bumpy  ≈ 1 magnitude brightening before transitioning to its eruption.

Industry observers note that evolution of FWHM velocities inferred from our spectra (red), compared to theoretical expectations for momentum-conserving collisions with CBM following a ρ(r) ∝ r−2 density profile (blue solid line). The broken lines indicate the expectation by including an additional mechanical power source, such as a surviving binary, injecting momentum into the ejecta. Our observations constrain the magnitude of this power source \(\mathop{E}\limits^{.}\lesssim 1{0}^{40}\) erg s−1.

It has been revealed that LRNe for which progenitor primary stars have been identified are plotted as coloured points, colour-coded by the binding energy of the star. LRNe with no progenitor identifications are plotted as grey points. The eruption of AT 2025abao (star) is remarkably similar to other LRNe, despite having a progenitor with the lowest binding energy ever measured.

Recent findings suggest that a, The quiescent binary system comprising a  ≈ 7 M⊙ AGB and a  ≈ 0.7 M⊙ star, surrounded by an extended dust shell from mass loss from the binary following Roche Lobe overflow of the primary. b, The precursor brightening phase that began in 2018, marking the onset of CEE, powered by frictional drag on the inspiraling companion lasting for  ≈ 7 years. The mass outflow rate during this phase is  ~10−2 M⊙ yr−1, producing  ~0.1 M⊙ of CBM in an equatorial disk around the binary (dark brown). c, The ballistic eruption in late 2025 from the merger of the inspiraling companion with the primary core, resulting in the ejection of  ≈ 0.1 − 0.2 M⊙ of the primary envelope, and sublimation of a large fraction of dust around the binary. d, The eventual lightcurve powered by shock-interactions between freely expanding merger ejecta (indicated by yellow arrows) and equatorially focused CBM. The surviving pre-existing dust is traced by our JWST observations. The black arrows between the panels indicate the progression of time.

During his press conference earlier today, Ruben Amorim spoke about Francesco Camarda and noted that the youngster appeared much happier after returning from international duty.

In a recent development, it hasn’t been an easy season for Camarda so far, getting a mere 119 minutes on the pitch, after initially believing that he would get a lot more. Luckily, he managed to boost his confidence during the international break, scoring for Italy’s U21 side against France.

Read SempreMilan ad-free and get access to exclusive news. Click here for a free trial!

He could perhaps use that to turn a corner, though everything depends on how much playing time Ruben Amorim is willing to give him. The feeling is that there isn’t loads up for grabs, which is why the loan rumours are heating up too.

During the press conference ahead of Milan-Frosinone earlier this afternoon, Amorim was asked about Camarda and what the next steps are for him. He confirmed that everything is up in the air, but also stated that the youngster is now in a much better mood.

Industry observers note that “I was a young player myself once too. A young player wants everything really badly, which is a good thing. That remarked, he needs time to adapt, it’s really hard to play for a club like Milan. You just said there is pressure on Ramos, imagine what it’s like for Camarda.

In a recent development, “I don’t know what will happen in January, but he needs to be focused on these games. Everything can change in just a few weeks.

Sources indicate that “I’m really happy with how he has been since he returned from international duty, I heard that Baldini spoke with him at length, and he returned in a happier mood. I understand the question about January, but January is so far away right now,” he stated.

It seems Silvio Baldini really did do wonders with his man-to-man talk with Camarda during the break.

  • A 1-0 win at the Houston Dynamo ensured St Louis finished third in the Western Conference MLS standings while Los Angeles wound up in sixth, losing 2-1 to the Seattle Sounders on Decision Day.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

By Joel Lefevre | 21 Nov 2026 18:37.

In search of their first MLS playoff victory, St Louis City will welcome Los Angeles FC to Energizer Park for game one of that best-of-three series on Monday.

A 1-0 win at the Houston Dynamo ensured St Louis finished third in the Western Conference MLS standings while Los Angeles wound up in sixth, losing 2-1 to the Seattle Sounders on Decision Day.

For the first time since their inaugural campaign in 2023, St Louis have made the post-season, finishing with 54 points in 2026.

Under Yoann Demet, this team earned 22 more points this year when compared to 2025 and were just two points short of equaling their best-ever campaign in 2023.

While they won nine regular-season affairs at Energizer Park this year, on Monday this team will try to snap a three-match MLS winless run at home, collecting just one point over that stretch.

St Louis have lost their only two playoff outings and have not been in front for a single second in any of those post-season fixtures.

During the regular season, they failed to lose a single league game at home when netting the opening goal, dropping points in only two of those instances.

In 2026, they had a perfect home record against the two LA clubs in MLS, holding on to a narrow 2-1 home win over LAFC in May.

Los Angeles FC were not satisfied with the direction they were heading in this fall, but their coaching change has made little difference.

Since Xavi Tamarit took over from Marc Dos Santos, the Black and Gold have claimed only one victory in league play and will try to avoid losing three straight matches to MLS teams on Monday for the second time this year.

Tamarit is still seeking his first domestic away triumph as the interim manager, while LAFC have not won an MLS away game since July against the Los Angeles Galaxy (3-0).

While they struggled on the road this season, the 2022 league champions have not lost in 90 minutes in their last two playoff outings as the visitors.

During the regular season, they conceded the second-fewest goals in the Western Conference (40) while averaging the third-fewest goals allowed per match in MLS (1.2).

The Black and Gold have earned points in seven of their eight all-time league meetings with St Louis City, including two wins and three clean sheets overall at Energizer Park.

St Louis City Major League Soccer form:.

St Louis City form (all competitions):.

Los Angeles FC Major League Soccer form:.

St Louis midfielder Carlo Holse is doubtful for game one due to a knee injury, Celio Pompeu is still recovering from a cruciate ligament tear, while Roman Burki will hope to return from concussion protocol.

Lukas MacNaughton had the only goal in their victory versus the Dynamo, and Ben Lundt made six stops to collect the clean sheet in place of Burki.

As for LAFC, Jacob Shaffelburg is unlikely to feature because of a rib fracture, Hugo Lloris is recovering from a rib injury of his own, Aaron Long has a head injury and Timothy Tillman is questionable due to a pelvic problem.

Son Heung-min has scored in his last three playoff games, while Eddie Segura had the only goal in their Decision Day defeat against Seattle.

St Louis City possible starting lineup:.

Burki; MacNaughton, Baumgartl, Fall; Wallem, Polvara, Durkin, Totland; Downs, Navarro, Ostrak.

Los Angeles FC possible starting lineup:.

Carter; Hollingshead, Porteous, Segura, Cheberko; Choiniere, Delgado; Sieb, Walta, Bouanga; Heung-min.

Neither side were all that convincing down the stretch of the regular season, but the visitors have some proven performers who have stepped it up in knockout matches, and we believe that experience will give LAFC a narrow win in game one.
