Could the AI boom make borrowing more expensive in Europe?

📅 03 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (865 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dw

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • With more than $1 trillion (€900 billion) pouring into the artificial intelligence (AI) buildout, US tech giants are now competing with governments and companies in Europe for the same investment capital.
  • Sources indicate that four of the Big Five hyperscalers — Amazon, Google owner Alphabet, Meta and Oracle — have issued about $250 billion in bonds in dollars since the beginning of 2025, according to a tally of filings to US financial regulators by AI Industry Reviews, an independent platform that evaluates AI tools.
  • Recently, Microsoft, the last of the Substantial Five to hold back, joined the AI borrowing spree with a $25 billion bond sale, all in dollars.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

With more than $1 trillion (€900 billion) pouring into the artificial intelligence (AI) buildout, US tech giants are now competing with governments and companies in Europe for the same investment capital.

Sources indicate that four of the Big Five hyperscalers — Amazon, Google owner Alphabet, Meta and Oracle — have issued about $250 billion in bonds in dollars since the beginning of 2025, according to a tally of filings to US financial regulators by AI Industry Reviews, an independent platform that evaluates AI tools. They have sold a further €37 billion ($41 billion) of bonds in euros.

Recently, Microsoft, the last of the Substantial Five to hold back, joined the AI borrowing spree with a $25 billion bond sale, all in dollars.

Next year, Goldman Sachs projects that total fresh AI hyperscaler bond sales are expected to reach $420 billion. About €60 billion will be issued in euros, according to Dutch bank ING.

That is unwelcome news for European companies and countries like France, Germany and Italy, whose sovereign bond yields have risen sharply in recent months and are already straining public finances.

Sources indicate that with public debt at 119% of gross domestic product (GDP) and a deficit still running above 5%, France is already paying a sizable risk premium on its debt. Over the past six months, yields on French 10-year bonds have climbed from roughly 3.7% to nearly 5%.

The French government's interest bill is set to rise from €79 billion currently to €91 billion next year and over €100 billion by 2028.

Based on these figures alone, France's Finance Ministry needs to find tens of billions of euros in additional cuts, tax hikes, or more borrowing by the end of the decade.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

In August, economists at the European Central Bank said the euro bond market was adapting well to the presence of AI giants but warned they "could make it harder for other companies and other economic sectors to access finance.".

Writing in a blog post, they also questioned whether the bloc's financial markets can "smoothly handle such large and concentrated debt inflows and warned of a "potential spillover to the sovereign and supranational segment of the bond market.".

That means governments and international lenders such as the European Union and the European Investment Bank could also end up paying more to borrow.

Viktor Hjort, global head of credit strategy at the French bank BNP Paribas, described the phenomenon as "bond abundance.".

Hjort told DW that the presence of the hyperscalers in the euro bond market is "already high enough to create competition" within the corporate sector and "between corporates and governments for available fixed income funds." These are investment funds that mostly buy bonds, which pay regular interest.

Bond yields jumped again last month, driven by rebounding energy prices linked to the Iran war and France’s political crisis, which Hjort said further revealed the growing competition for capital, as government and tech giant borrowing costs rose together.

Normally, nervous investors move into government bonds during uncertain times, which pushes their borrowing costs down.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

Goldman Sachs warned last week that rising interest costs were starting to hurt earnings at European companies. Among firms in the Stoxx 600 — an index of 600 large, mid-sized and small companies across Europe — Goldman found that interest costs as a share of sales have risen by nearly half since 2022.

The bank's analysts said this had cut earnings by more than 5% over the same period.

Factor in the competition from AI bonds, and European firms could now face pressure to cut their investments in fresh plants, equipment and research, as well as shareholder payouts, to prioritize loan repayments.

Recent findings suggest that the pressure doesn't stop at national governments. Europe's cities and regions, whose borrowing helps to fund schools, transport and infrastructure, may also feel the effects of the AI boom.

Industry observers note that A study for the Organization for Economic Co-operation and Development(OECD), published in January, compared local bond markets in Belgium, Germany, Spain, Sweden and Canada. Where AI was spreading fastest, measured by the share of AI-related job vacancies, borrowing costs for cities and regions tended to rise.

Recent findings suggest that "Whereas in the United States, my research has found that AI investments are linked to a lower cost of borrowing for municipalities, the opposite appears to hold in several European countries," the study's co-author, Christos Makridis of Arizona State University's W. P. Carey School of Business, told DW.

While AI bonds are far from the sole cause of Europe's widening fiscal strains, US Massive Tech's huge appetite for capital could add further pressure next year, due to the additional billions in new bonds planned.

The irony is that European taxpayers could end up paying more on their own governments' debt, partly to help finance an AI boom across the Atlantic.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

By Ben Sully | 21 Nov 2026 18:44.

Bournemouth set a fresh club record by claiming a 2-0 victory over Nottingham Forest on Saturday afternoon.

After carrying an eight-game winning run into the international break, Bournemouth returned to action with another successful outing in their home meeting with Oliver Glasner's side.

Evanilson opened the scoring just shy of the 20-minute mark, before Justin Kluivert scored what proved to be the game's final goal in first-half stoppage time.

As a result, Bournemouth have now won nine consecutive games in all competitions for the first time in their history.

They have claimed five of those victories in the Premier League, two in the Europa League and one in the EFL Cup.

Their current run of form has surpassed two separate eight-game winning streaks they enjoyed in 1998-99 and 2012-13.

What makes Bournemouth's run all the more impressive is the fact they have recorded seven clean sheets in their last nine games, representing a remarkable improvement from the side that shipped five goals against Chelsea on October 10.

When asked about Bournemouth's historic run, Rose told BBC Match of the Day: "We are not looking for records, we are just looking for the next game and talking about the next game.

"We took the right approach. We were ready for this game, We knew it would be tough and we would have to stay patient, and that's what we did, especially in the first half, really well.

"That is why it was a top performance and a deserved win.".

In a recent development, first six PL games this season: LDDDLL Next five PL games: WWWWW Marco Rose is cooking. ?‍?

Evanilson has netted seven goals in Bournemouth's winning run, including one in each of his last five competitive appearances.

In fact, the Brazilian has scored in six successive top-flight matches, making it the longest scoring streak in Bournemouth's Premier League history.

Praising his star striker, Rose stated: "The way he works for us out of possession, works as a link player and goes deep. The way he scores is quite impressive.".

After climbing up to fourth spot in the Premier League table, Bournemouth will now turn their focus towards Thursday's Europa League away clash against Celta Vigo.

Much more of this and the adjectives which were splattered across Chelsea during the golden years of José Mourinho – solid, robust and dogged – will be part of the Stamford Bridge lexicon once more.

According to recent reports, yet the true catalyst for the resurgence was the return of Moises Caicedo. Recent findings suggest that next up is a notoriously difficult trip to Merseyside to face Everton in Saturday’s lunchtime fixture. Historically, Everton have proven to be a formidable stumbling block for the capital club, particularly on home turf. Everton enter the weekend unbeaten in eight of their last nine home encounters against Chelsea, a stretch that has seen the Londoners fail to score on seven visits and suffer six defeats, including a chastening 3-0 reverse last term that spelt the end for Liam Rosenior.

Recent findings suggest that david Moyes will demand a sharper defensive showing from his side this time around, following a frustrating 2-2 draw with Hull City where a 2-1 lead slipped away. Even so, Everton’s broader defensive record at home offers encouragement, having kept clean sheets in two of their opening three league fixtures at their base.

With both teams eager to build consistency, Saturday’s clash pits Chelsea’s newly found attacking spark against an opponent that traditionally relishes this fixture.

Asian Cup postponed due to Middle East conflict

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A little over two months before it was set to kick off, the Asian Football Confederation (AFC) has postponed its flagship international football tournament in the wake of recent deadly attacks on host country, Saudi Arabia.
  • The AFC cited "substantial logistical complexities and travel disruptions" caused by conflicts in the region.
  • Instead of January 7, 2027, the tournament will now kick off on December 23 and end on January 21, 2028.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A little over two months before it was set to kick off, the Asian Football Confederation (AFC) has postponed its flagship international football tournament in the wake of recent deadly attacks on host country, Saudi Arabia.

The AFC cited "substantial logistical complexities and travel disruptions" caused by conflicts in the region.

Instead of January 7, 2027, the tournament will now kick off on December 23 and end on January 21, 2028. The postponement follows delays and cancellations of a number of sporting events in the region, including a Formula One race, the men's and women's tennis finals, the 2027 Dakar Rally and disruption to Asia's marquee continental club football tournament, the AFC Champions League Elite.

Saudi Arabia hosted, and won, the Gulf Cup last month, but there had already been much talk about whether the much larger Asian Cup could go ahead.

It was scheduled to feature 24 teams playing matches in eight venues across Riyadh, Jeddah and Khobar. However, the AFC said that "circumstances arising from developments in the region, including substantial logistical complexities and travel disruptions," made the tournament impossible.

"Exceptional circumstances have been created for the organization and delivery of the competition as originally scheduled, making the postponement necessary in the interest of all participating teams, officials, spectators and other stakeholders.".

In particular, the postponement was forced by a recent wave of deadly attacks on Saudi Arabia by Iran-backed Houthi rebels as well as other raging conflicts in the region. The Houthis have targeted Saudi infrastructure, including airports. They are fighting a Saudi-led coalition supporting Yemen's internationally recognized government, a civil war that reignited in July following a years-long truce.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

The AFC had been under pressure from several federations to postpone the tournament, with South Korea's players leading the way.

"The ongoing military tensions and security instability in the Middle East are concerns that cannot be taken lightly," Lee Keun-ho, president of the Korea Professional Footballers Association, said last month, according to the Yonhap News Agency.

Lee added that "no tournament's value can take precedence over the lives and safety of players and football fans.".

Recent findings suggest that it seems that the AFC now agrees. However, following the announcement of the postponement, Yasser al-Misehal, chairman of the local organizing committee, promised that Saudi Arabia was "fully ready" whenever the tournament ended up being held.

"The tournament will move to the fresh dates, and our preparations will continue as planned," he told the Saudi Press Agency.

"We're working closely with the AFC and all our partners to make sure the tournament runs smoothly and meets the high standards expected of Saudi Arabia and the Asian Cup.".

Saudi Arabia has invested hugely in sports over the last decade, from owning Premier League teams to hosting boxing title fights and bidding for a number of major sporting events, most notably World Cup 2034, which they won the right to host unopposed.

However, the country has recently withdrawn or slashed funding for a number of sporting events including golf, rugby, tennis and winter sports.

Ruben Amorim will be up against Massimiliano Alvini tomorrow evening, and as the stats show, they are two very different managers.

It has been revealed that as highlighted by Gazzetta dello Sport, there is one interesting stat to highlight to introduce the game. In terms of shots per game, it will be the second-ranked team and against the 17th-ranked team. That in itself won’t raise any eyebrows, but the fact that Milan are the ones in 17th place will.

It has been revealed that read SempreMilan ad-free and get access to exclusive news. Click here for a free trial!

Recent findings suggest that the Rossoneri have mustered a mere 126 shots so far, while Frosinone are quite far ahead at 221. On the flip side, the newly-promoted side have only scored one more goal than Milan (24 vs. 23), which is what makes this game so interesting.

Industry observers note that amorim has made it clear from the start that he wants to dominate each game. That shows in the possession, as Milan are third in Serie A with an average of 59% so far, and they also rank high in terms of passes per game.

The shots are where they fall short, even if they average over two goals per game. There are several reasons for this, but most of it can be attributed to Amorim’s recent arrival and the fact that he has experimented rather extensively.

During today’s presser, he even said that they haven’t done anywhere near enough to enter the penalty box more often, which tends to mean more shots.

Recent findings suggest that in the build-up, for example, the Rossoneri move the ball forward at an average speed of 1.30 meters per second, which is the slowest in Serie A. Alvini’s Frosinone, on the other hand, are great at vertical football: the ball moves toward the opponent’s penalty box at 2.51 meters per second, the best rate in the league.

Industry observers note that the Ciociari are masters of rapid counterattacks, so much so that on only 40 occasions have they built plays with ten or more passes. Milan, meanwhile, have 203.

In a recent development, everything starts in the defence phase for Frosinone. Indeed, they always attempt to win the ball back inside the opponent’s half, which is proven by the index that measures the intensity of pressing in the attacking zone (they are first in Serie A).

According to recent reports, milan? They are eighth, despite being – along with Como – the team to have scored the most goals (4) from a ball recovered while pressing.

The difference between the two is well explained by the so-called “pressed sequences”, that is, the number of actions in open play in which a team manages to interrupt the opponent’s build-up within three passes or less, before the ball goes beyond the halfway line.

On that front, Frosinone are also first (161), while Milan are only 15th (102). Having mentioned all of this, as the pink newspaper concludes, we should expect a spectacular match tomorrow. Both teams will stick to their respective game, which bodes well.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Richard Hughes made a lot of mistakes when he was Liverpool's sporting director.

The Englishman spent well over £600 million on new players and, it's still unclear whether their team is any better off.

So, even though Hughes did quite well with some of the deals he made, he obviously had to make a few mistakes on the way.

Right now, Liverpool's entire team could still do with upgrading but, because they have a handful of players who's contract are going to expire in June 2027, they've taken priority.

The January transfer window is now just over a month away so, some transfers are going to have to take place soon, otherwise, the Reds will be left even further behind their title rivals than they currently find themselves.

Julian Ward can sign Luka Vuskovic after Richard Hughes chose against it in the summer.

Liverpool's defence has been one of the main areas that Liverpool have tried to strengthen over the last few years.

Virgil van Dijk, Andy Robertson and Joe Gomez are just a few examples of the older players that they were using last season.

And, with Robertson gone and the other two having their contracts expire in June 2027, another defensive rebuild could be on the way.

Many different links with players have emerged recently with Giorgio Scalvini one of them.

However, a recent patch from Florian Plettenberg on Luka Vuskovic's situation is something that should definitely pique the interest of Liverpool and their fanbase.

"Liverpool have Luka Vuskovic on their shortlist for next summer. The 19 y/o top defender is being monitored regularly," he shared via X.

"His contract at Brighton is valid until 2031. No release clause will be available next summer. Current price valuation: around €100m (+/-).

According to recent reports, "Vuskovic is very happy under Fabian Hürzeler. However, his dream is to join Real Madrid one day.

Liverpool need to sign Luka Vuskovic.

Vuskovic has been a revelation since joining Brighton.

The Croatian had a spectacular season last term while on loan with Hamburger SV with most people thinking that Tottenham would welcome him back with open arms.

However, that didn't end up happening and, instead of keeping the 19-year-old around, Roberto de Zerbi chose to bring Jan Paul Van Hecke through the welcome doors instead.

And, while the Dutchman's performances have been impressive, Vuskovic has probably been the better player.

He's transformed Fabian Hurzeler's defence and, there's no wonder why the Seagulls want a record deal for the centre-back.

Obviously, it's a lot of money to spend on a defender who's only had one season of Premier League experience but, if they did manage to get a deal over the line, Ward would be instantly rectifying a problem that Hughes made for himself.

It would also be a sure-fire way for the Englishman to get fans on his side as, during the summer, most Liverpool fans wanted their club to sign him.

Newcastle 2-2 Arsenal: Highlights, man of the match, stats as Noni Madueke rescues complacent champions

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (855 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Co

💡 Key Takeaways
  • By Ben Knapton | 21 Nov 2026 19:30, Last updated: 21 Nov 2026 20:07.
  • Arsenal spurned the chance to go eight points clear at the top of the Premier League table as they were forced to come from behind to draw 2-2 with Newcastle United at St James' Park.
  • Warned to expect a "hellish" fixture at a ground where they have not had much luck in recent years, the champions were in the ascendancy from the off and deservedly went into half time ahead courtesy of Eberechi Eze's first-time finish.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

By Ben Knapton | 21 Nov 2026 19:30, Last updated: 21 Nov 2026 20:07.

Arsenal spurned the chance to go eight points clear at the top of the Premier League table as they were forced to come from behind to draw 2-2 with Newcastle United at St James' Park.

Warned to expect a "hellish" fixture at a ground where they have not had much luck in recent years, the champions were in the ascendancy from the off and deservedly went into half time ahead courtesy of Eberechi Eze's first-time finish.

Matthias Jaissle's men were booed off at half time after generating just 0.08 Expected Goals during the opening period, but that number shot up just four minutes into the second half, when a gift from Martin Odegaard handed Harvey Barnes an equaliser against the run of play.

Barnes's strike triggered a magnificent Newcastle response, one that saw them rewarded with the game's third goal through Malick Thiaw just past the hour mark following a corner scramble.

However, the momentum pendulum swung back Arsenal's way shortly after, as the effervescent Noni Madueke drew the holders level to set up a grand-stand finish.

Nine minutes of added time was not enough for either team to snatch a winner, as Arsenal extended their lead over Manchester City and Brighton & Hove Albion to six points, while Newcastle remain 12th with 13 points.

For all of Arsenal's first-half dominance, the Gunners were guilty of a perpetual shortcoming in the Arteta era; not putting the game to bed before the break.

Staunch Newcastle defending and shoddy Arsenal finishing denied the visitors a healthier first-half advantage, and while the champions cut complacent figures at the start of the second half, Jaissle's half-time team talk worked a treat.

Odegaard's blunder helped the hosts on their way, and Arsenal found themselves unfamiliarly rattled for a good 30 minutes, until the increasingly impressive Madueke came to the fore again.

However, the winger himself admitted that his side should have been at least three to the good at half time, yet more evidence that a killer finisher is a matter of priority for the January transfer window.

Recent findings suggest that "Absolutely clinical!" Eberechi Eze scores his first Premier League goal of the season to give Arsenal the lead ? https://t.co/34IbZuuJuN.

Seven months after his last Premier League goal - against the Magpies - the Englishman does it again, rifling in a slick side-footed strike from 12 yards after Kai Havertz's delightful through ball.

Havertz had robbed Lewis Hall of possession before slipping in Eze, who left Lukas Hornicek rooted to the spot.

"Horrendous error!" Harvey Barnes puts Newcastle level ? https://t.co/YWrHZPxBIo.

A howler from Odegaard, a flicker of hope for Newcastle!

The Arsenal captain tries to volley a throw-in close to his own penalty area, but gets his connection all wrong and slices the ball into William Osula's path.

The Newcastle striker spots Barnes in acres of space in the left of the box, and the latter takes one touch to set himself before calmly slotting home into the bottom corner!

Malick Thiaw is in the right place to fire it in and give Newcastle the lead against Arsenal! ? https://t.co/nthaH3aOJD.

When we talk about a game of two halves, this is exactly what we mean.

Dan Burn finds himself all alone as a corner is floated in; replays show that Jurrien Timber - his marker - was being held back by Osula as he tried to catch up to him.

The towering Newcastle defender heads the ball back into the danger area, and after an almighty scramble, Thiaw pokes home from a yard out!

In a recent development, noni Madueke equalises for Arsenal! ? https://t.co/VNXOoNDxiJ.

Champions respond how champions respond.

Odegaard just broke down a counter-attack by picking the wrong pass, but the Arsenal captain gets it right this time, laying off Madueke on the right-hand side.

The winger cuts inside, works a yard for a shot from inside the D, and the ball finds its way into the bottom corner via Hornicek's gloves.

The Newcastle goalkeeper ought to have done better, but credit the free-flowing move from the visitors, who are level again!

"I reckon 2-2 was a fair result." Noni Madueke reflects on Arsenal's performance against Newcastle at St James' Park ? https://t.co/UfDi5SGgat.

Both frustrating and fascinating to watch for Arsenal fans, Madueke once again proved a capable deputy for Bukayo Saka on the right.

The England international had six shots in total, made one key pass and registered four successful dribbles, albeit while missing two big chances that could, or should, have been the difference between Arsenal taking home either one or three points.

Possession: Newcastle 34%-66% Arsenal.

Shots on target: Newcastle 3-4 Arsenal.

Harvey Barnes for Newcastle: 50 G/A 35 goals 15 assists https://t.co/3TMxbJSB7i.

Arsenal resume their Champions League campaign at home to Borussia Dortmund on Tuesday evening, before the major one against Manchester City in next Sunday's Premier League showdown.

Meanwhile, Newcastle have over a week to recuperate before they travel to Arsenal's closest Premier League title challengers Brighton & Hove Albion next Sunday.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Published: 21:00 EST, 20 November 2026 | Updated: 21:00 EST, 20 November 2026.
  • Some grounds take you to the heart of the English game.
  • But each of them holds the soul of their community and the hopes and dreams of the thousands of people who make the pilgrimage there every weekend.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Published: 21:00 EST, 20 November 2026 | Updated: 21:00 EST, 20 November 2026.

Some grounds are beautiful. Some grounds are not so beautiful. Some grounds take you to the heart of the English game. And some leave you feeling like you're on the periphery.

But each of them holds the soul of their community and the hopes and dreams of the thousands of people who make the pilgrimage there every weekend.

Industry observers note that on April 1, 2025, I made the trip to Harrogate Town’s Exercise Stadium and first fulfilled the quest of a lifetime by completing the set of all 92 English Football League grounds for Daily Mail Sport. But then Everton moved away from Goodison Park and into a stunning new stadium on the banks of the River Mersey.

It has been revealed that I was one short again but on February 23, 2026, I got back up to 92 by going to Hill Dickinson Stadium to watch Everton versus Manchester United. Then, in November, with York City being promoted (alongside Rochdale, whose ground I had ticked off decades ago), I made the trip to the LNER Stadium to make the 92 whole again.

Recent findings suggest that I won’t give too much away just yet, but why are grounds like AFC Wimbledon and Exeter City in my top 20? What about Anfield, Old Trafford and Stamford Bridge? Where does Everton’s dazzling new home rank? Where is the best grub in the Premier League and where did Tyson Fury once threaten to have my jaw broken?

Recent findings suggest that this is my love letter to English football. Read on to find out who comes out on top, where your team ranks and everything else in between – then let me know what you think of my guide to the 92 grounds of England.

Division: Championship Opened: 1993 Capacity: 19,369.

Being banned from The Den is the football equivalent of being banned from your local abattoir.

Sources indicate that I’ve been banned from The Den for the last 20 months, in a professional capacity anyway. I could still go in a personal capacity but, on balance, I think I’d rather not.

The Daily Mail has been told that our reporters are not welcome at the club because we had the temerity to report on the horrendous challenge by Millwall goalkeeper Liam Roberts on Crystal Palace’s Jean-Philippe Mateta during the FA Cup tie at Selhurst Park in March last year, which left the French striker requiring 25 stitches in his left ear.

Let’s be honest about this: there are worse places to be banned from. Being banned from The Den is the football equivalent of being banned from your local abattoir. You don’t have to be a racist, misogynistic, homophobic bloke with anger problems and a penchant for tragedy-chanting to feel at home at The Den. But it helps.

And, yes, I know Millwall are trying to rebrand themselves as a ‘family club’ now and the odd Tarquin and Tabitha stray across the county lines from Blackheath and Clapham to keep it real but that just makes The Den experience even worse.

The last time I went as a supporter was 16 years ago to watch Stockport County play there and the walk from South Bermondsey station to the away turnstiles was an eye-opener.

It has been revealed that not that there were any problems: even at Millwall, football has moved on since the 70s. But this still felt deeply dystopian: for their own safety, away fans walk to the ground through a long wire mesh cage that seems to have no end. It felt like embarking on a tour of Jurassic Park: you know that if the fences fail, the dinosaurs are going to take a run at you.

Recent findings suggest that inside the ground, which is modern and neat and relatively characterless, the level of hatred for visiting supporters feels unusually visceral. It’s loud. I’ll give it that. It’s primeval. It’s unreconstructed, which can be a good thing, too, and it breeds a sense of togetherness.

Sources indicate that if medievalism is your thing, you’re in for a treat. If not, give it a miss.

Division: League One Opened: 2007 Capacity: 30,303.

Recent findings suggest that I know it’s a soft target but I really don’t care much for Stadium MK. Or for MK Dons, for that matter.

According to recent reports, I know it’s a soft target but I really don’t care much for Stadium MK. Or for MK Dons themselves for that matter.

Recent findings suggest that the club was born under a bad sign when it was jemmied out of Wimbledon and moved to Milton Keynes in 2003 and it has never been able to shake the stigma since. The stadium fits the club.

It has been revealed that it is a soulless, faceless, gloomy place. More than that, there is something rather forbidding about it. Its 30,000 capacity is too massive for the club it hosts and, apart from the joys of the local KFC and McDonald’s, there is little to recommend in its immediate surrounds. Its black seats lend it a sinister air, too.

Recent findings suggest that it’s the kind of stadium only its mother could love. And it doesn’t have a mother. Unless you want to do the 92, give it a miss.

Sources indicate that 90. Kassam Stadium, Oxford United.

Division: League One Opened: 2001 Capacity: 12,537.

The empty end kills a lot of the atmosphere, although the Oxford fans are to be commended for the noise they do generate.

I feel ashamed to say it, given that it is my local club, but the best experience I’ve had at the Kassam Stadium was getting my Covid jab there during the pandemic.

When they moved, around the turn of the century, abandoning the chaotic charm of the Manor Ground in Headington and swapping it for an isolated plateau outside the city, they only completed three sides, abandoning the fourth because of rising costs.

A particularly bitter wind blows in off the car park behind one of the goals and, from the main stand – in fact, from every stand – there is a magnificent and uninterrupted view of the Frankie and Benny's in the mini retail park that abuts the ground.

Industry observers note that the empty end kills a lot of the atmosphere, too, although the Oxford fans are to be commended for the noise they do generate given they have endured a generation of being stuck here. Firoz Kassam still owns the stadium but not the club. That kind of separation always spells trouble.

Oxford are hoping to move to a latest stadium to the north of the city in a couple of years’ time. It can’t come soon enough.

89. London Stadium, West Ham United.

Division: Championship Opened: 2012 Capacity: 62,500.

It was a great athletics arena and home to a whole host of golden memories at London 2012 but it’s a dog’s dinner of a football ground.

Sources indicate that I don’t even like calling it the London Stadium. It’s the Olympic Stadium, but it suited the David Sullivan-Karren Brady rebrand of the club to give it the capital’s name.

Recent findings suggest that it was a great athletics arena and home to a whole host of golden memories at London 2012 but it’s a dog’s dinner of a football ground. It’s also a monument to much that is wrong with the upper reaches of the English game: a surrender of identity and tradition as collateral damage in the owners’ pursuit of profit.

Sources indicate that walking to it, sadly, feels a bit like walking through a wasteland and its odd configuration inside harms the atmosphere even though the fans are right up there with the best in the country. The old stadium at Upton Park was intimate and raucous and intimidating. The London Stadium is nothing like that.

The owners spent a lot of time congratulating themselves on the deal they did to move to the latest ground: they’re the archetypes of football owners who know the price of everything and the value of nothing.

88. Hillsborough, Sheffield Wednesday.

Division: League One Opened: 1899 Capacity: 34,835.

It is hard to get past Hillsborough's association with so much death and despair and heartbreak and the betrayal of supporters.

I used to think of Hillsborough as one of the cathedrals of the English game but since the disaster that claimed the lives of 97 Liverpool fans in 1989, it is hard to get past its association with so much death and despair and heartbreak and betrayal of supporters.

I know, obviously, that this would punish Wednesday fans who do not deserve to be punished for something that had nothing to do with them but Hillsborough, and its Leppings Lane End in particular, has such a cursed legacy that part of me thinks it should have been demolished and that the club should have moved elsewhere.

Even in the last couple of years, fans of Newcastle United and Leeds United have reported serious safety concerns in the Leppings Lane End.

I recognise the flaws in my argument about demolishing the stadium, or part of it, and the emotions it provokes on all sides so perhaps it’s just enough to say I’ll never feel the same about the stadium as I once did.

Visiting it now feels like an intrusion.

It has been revealed that 87. Sixfields, Northampton Town.

Division: League Two Opened: 1994 Capacity: 8,203.

Sixfields is a soulless ground anyway but its issues have been compounded by redevelopment delays and questions about missing money.

Sixfields is a blighted stadium.

It is a soulless ground anyway but its issues have been compounded by redevelopment delays and questions about missing money.

In a recent development, it has the same kind of deracinated feel as so many of the latest-build stadia pushed to the peripheries of towns. Its supporters deserve a lot better.

In a recent development, 86. Broadfield Stadium, Crawley Town.

Division: League Two Opened: 1997 Capacity: 5,907.

If you visit the Broadfield Stadium, I think you might doubt if Crawley are even in League Two.

Not an awful lot to relish about the Broadfield Stadium, to be honest.

Decent fans, of course, just like at every club, but Crawley Town’s home is a bit of a modern monstrosity, next to a roundabout outside town on the A23.

It has been revealed that if you visit the Broadfield Stadium, I think you might doubt if Crawley are even in League Two. I had fun when I visited because I was in the away end with Stockport fans but I’m not in any hurry to go back.

Sources indicate that 85. Coventry Building Society Arena, Coventry City.

Division: Premier League Opened: 2005 Capacity: 32,609.

Football at the CBS Arena feels like it is in an urban wasteland but it is football, nonetheless.

When it was called the Ricoh Arena, I had no interest in visiting what is now the Coventry Building Society Arena because it felt like a symbol of the callous way in which fans of the club were being treated by SISU, the hedge fund that owned it at the time.

But SISU sold up in the end and I went along a few years back to see Coventry dismantle Wayne Rooney’s Birmingham City. Then, in the press room beneath the stadium, I watched as my colleague Neil Moxley got into a decent old-fashioned row with Rooney about his stewardship of the Blues.

The atmosphere inside the ground was lively enough, partly because the game was a derby of sorts, but it is a soulless stadium abutting the M6.

It is football in an urban wasteland but it is football, nonetheless, and Doug King, the upcoming owner, has brought with him much better times.

Recent findings suggest that 84. JobServe Community Stadium, Colchester United.

Division: League Two Opened: 2008 Capacity: 10,105.

This stadium on a roundabout on the A12 in the middle of a retail park is rather a bleak place to watch football.

The staff at the club are great, the stewards are friendly, there's plenty of parking, there's a Wendy's next door and the home fans, largely arranged in a stand behind one of the goals, make a superb first of creating an atmosphere.

But this stadium on a roundabout on the A12 in the middle of a retail park is still rather a bleak place to watch football.

It probably didn’t help that I went on a dank March night when a wispy fog lingered in the dim floodlight glare but there was something ethereally gloomy about the JobServe Community Stadium.

The empty corridors and the cavernous suites lent it a slight feel of the Overlook Hotel on the inside. On the outside, the four corners of the stadium are open, which makes for especially bitter nights in the winter.

Home is home and there was still plenty of drama and passion in Colchester’s 1-0 victory over Chesterfield – the match I saw – but it came despite the stadium, not because of it.

83. Pallet-Track Bescot Stadium, Walsall.

Division: League Two Opened: 1990 Capacity: 10,863.

The Bescot Stadium was the first of the generation of identikit latest-build arenas I went to and there is not, frankly, much to recommend it apart from the loyalty of the fans.

The Bescot was the first of the generation of identikit upcoming-build arenas I went to and there is not, frankly, much to recommend it apart from the loyalty of the fans.

It’s close to the M6 and it’s a seven-minute walk to Walsall station – so you can get away from it promptly, which some would say is a bonus.

It has been revealed that 82. Brick Community Stadium, Wigan Athletic.

Division: League One Opened: 1999 Capacity: 25,133.

The name changes are irrelevant to some but they betray a lack of care for the identity of a football club.

I stood on the terraces at Springfield Park as a Stockport fan.

Once again, it will not come as a surprise to learn I preferred it to its successor, the JJB Stadium, which later became the DW Stadium and is now the Brick Community Stadium.

The name changes are irrelevant to some but they betray a lack of care for the identity of a football club.

There were some great days and nights there when Wigan were promoted to the Premier League and I remember, in particular, the heady feeling of watching Wigan’s first home game in the top flight, against Jose Mourinho’s Chelsea in 2005.

The limelight has moved away again now and Wigan are left with a stadium that is perfectly adequate and also perfectly unremarkable.

According to recent reports, 81. The Croud Meadow, Shrewsbury Town.

Division: League Two Opened: 2007 Capacity: 9,875.

Abutted by a McDonald’s and a TK Maxx on the outer fringes of the town, it feels like a disembodied place, separated from its community, functional but uninspired.

Gay Meadow, the former home of Shrewsbury Town, was one of the best grounds in our top four divisions.

It might have flooded now and again because of its position on the banks of the River Severn but it was a fine old ground and the tradition of a boatman taking to a coracle to fish wayward shots that cleared the roof of the stand out of the river was one of the most cherished peculiarities in our game.

According to recent reports, the Croud Meadow is altogether more prosaic. Abutted by a McDonald’s and a TK Maxx on the outer fringes of the town, it feels like a disembodied place, separated from its community, functional but uninspired.

Industry observers note that 80. Select Car Leasing Stadium, Reading.

Division: League One Opened: 1998 Capacity: 24,376.

I was persona non grata for a while at the Select Car Leasing Stadium when I took exception to Reading taking out two Chelsea goalkeepers in one match back in 2006.

I was persona non grata for a while at the Select Car Leasing Stadium when I took exception to Reading taking out two Chelsea goalkeepers in one match back in 2006, when Steve Coppell and Wally Downes were in charge at the Madejski Stadium.

People called it the Mad Stad back then and I remember Neil Warnock telling me about being chased to his car outside the main entrance when he was manager of Sheffield United.

And Wally took a swing at me at a Football Writers’ Association dinner a couple of years later.

Anyway, I’ve made up with Stephen Hunt, who was one of the players involved in the tumult against Chelsea, and with Downes since then.

Even if the Mad Stad doesn’t have an awful lot of personality, I have only respect for the Reading fans who endured so much under the ownership of Dai Yongge and fought for their club.

In a recent development, 79. Pride Park Stadium, Derby County.

Division: Championship Opened: 1997 Capacity: 32,956.

Too many of the modern bowls have lost character because the fans just merge into one.

Pride Park is the standard-bearer, sadly, for what is lacking in many of the new generation of English football stadia.

English football grounds should be about the North Bank and the Stretford End and the Kop and the Gallowgate End and the Shelf.

They’re supposed to be about defined areas that give a stadium character and personality and even rivalry among home fans about who sings loudest.

Too many of the modern bowls have lost that character because the fans just merge into one.

Recent findings suggest that this is not a criticism of Derby County fans in any way. They still make plenty of noise inside their stadium but the place is not a patch on the Baseball Ground, which witnessed so many momentous days and nights.

Pride Park is bland and featureless, a symbol of its team’s current struggle for identity as it languishes near the foot of the Championship.

78. Swansea.com Stadium, Swansea City.

Division: Championship Opened: 2003 Capacity: 20,996.

The Swansea.com Stadium lacks character but is a tight ground where the fans can still generate a rousing atmosphere if their team’s displays allow it.

My in-laws used to live in Swansea and when I wasn’t out walking to Worm’s Head at Rhossili or enjoying the delights of Mumbles and the Wales Coast Path, I’d make the occasional pilgrimage to what was left of the Vetch Field.

According to recent reports, I stood in the away end there with Manchester United fans in the early 80s but when I visited later in my life, the Vetch was locked up and derelict. If you peered through the gates, you could see small trees and shrubs growing on the pitch.

The Swansea.com Stadium lacks the same character, obviously, but it is a tight ground where the fans can still generate a rousing atmosphere if their team’s displays allow it.

Sources indicate that I did a phone interview with Mike Tyson from the press box here a couple of hours before a game once. I couldn’t hear him very well because of various announcements being made over the loud-speaker system and soon, his tone became rather impatient but still, a conversation with Mike Tyson in the press box at Swansea is not easily forgotten.

77. Pirelli Stadium, Burton Albion.

Division: League One Opened: 2005 Capacity: 7,088.

Burton’s a fine club with a distinguished non-League history that can boast Neil Warnock and Nigel Clough as former managers and which has nailed down its place in the Football League.

The main entrance of the Pirelli Stadium looks a little like a car showroom. The rest of it struggles for character, too.

Burton’s a fine club with a distinguished non-League history that can boast Neil Warnock and Nigel Clough as former managers and which has nailed down its place in the Football League.

It has been a club to be admired for a long time, particularly under the former stewardship of Ben Robinson, who sold his majority stake to the Nordic Football Group.

They have punched above their weight for much of that time and their stadium is built for practicality, not for artistic merit.

76. Vitality Stadium, Bournemouth.

Division: Premier League Opened: 1910 Capacity: 11,307.

Recent findings suggest that it’s a bit of a Lego arena, sure, but it’s built for its audience and its catchment area. It’s a League Two stadium that got overtaken by the success of its side.

The club is one of the success stories of modern English football and the Vitality Stadium reflects its enthusiasm and, yes, vitality.

In a recent development, it’s a bit of a Lego arena, sure, but it’s built for its audience and its catchment area. It’s a League Two stadium that got overtaken by the success of its side.

Its character comes from its small size and the atmosphere it generates because of it.

Abutting King’s Park and not far from the sea front, it’s a ground that almost manages to feel quaint. But not quite.

75. Club Doncaster Sports Village, Doncaster Rovers.

Division: League One Opened: 2007 Capacity: 15,148.

This is a uniform modern bowl on the outside of town rescued by the club’s excellent support.

It is, at least, a pleasant walk to the stadium on the outskirts of Doncaster.

I parked on the estate grouped around Lakeside Lake and strolled around its shores until I came to the stadium. Things go slightly downhill from there.

According to recent reports, it’s a perfectly presentable stadium but there is little to distinguish it. It is a uniform modern bowl stuck on the outside of town that is rescued by the club’s excellent support.

74. St Mary's Stadium, Southampton.

Division: Championship Opened: 2001 Capacity: 32,384.

It doesn’t feel as though Southampton's St Mary’s Stadium has any quirks, unfortunately.

Squatting at the edge of a slightly murky industrial estate, it falls squarely into the category of new-builds largely devoid of character.

Southampton’s former ground, The Dell, was a wonderfully quirky stadium, full of odd tiers and shelves.

It doesn’t feel as though St Mary’s Stadium has any quirks, unfortunately.

Squatting at the edge of a slightly murky industrial estate, it falls squarely into the category of new-builds largely devoid of character.

That does not mean that the home fans are incapable of creating atmosphere there and the renditions of When the Saints Go Marching In are a part of the cultural fabric of football in this country.

Sight lines are good and it can get loud but its design has little to recommend it.

73. King Power Stadium, Leicester City.

Division: League One Opened: 2002 Capacity: 32,259.

It is comfortable and it is functional and the Leicester fans can make plenty of noise but it’s a bland, featureless bowl that has little to distinguish it from many of the new era of stadia.

One of the few times I was genuinely scared at a football stadium when I was a supporter was during a visit to Leicester City’s former stadium at Filbert Street.

In the crush to get out of the away end at the final whistle, I was lifted off my feet in the surge.

So I’m aware that there are limits to how much one should mourn the passing of that generation of stadia but I still find it hard to warm to arenas like the King Power.

It is comfortable and it is functional and the Leicester fans made plenty of noise in happier times but it’s a bland, featureless bowl that has little to distinguish it from many of the new generation of stadia.

Even then, it provided me with one of the great memories of the last decade when Andrea Bocelli stood next to Claudio Ranieri and sang Nessun Dorma the game after Leicester had pulled off the shock of the century by winning the Premier League in 2016.

Division: League One Opened: 1961 Capacity: 7,426.

Broadhall Way is a decent little ground with a good atmosphere, and home to a friendly club.

Broadhall Way, now known as the SPORTA Arena, is a decent little ground with a good atmosphere.

And it is home to a fine club, one that has consistently achieved more than most expected of it and has held down its place in the Football League.

The Stevenage fans create more than their share of noise but it’s a friendly club with great staff and stewards.

It’s not spectacular but it’s a lovely day out watching football.

Recent findings suggest that 71. EV Charger Points Stadium, Cheltenham Town.

Division: League Two Opened: 1927 Capacity: 6,923.

EV Charger Points Stadium may have the most chequered naming rights past of any stadium in the country.

It is a high bar in these days when money counts a lot more than heritage and finances are fraught at the wrong end of the EFL, but the EV Charger Points Stadium may have the most chequered naming rights past of any stadium in the country.

We should just stick with Whaddon Road really but it was renamed the Abbey Business Stadium in 2009, then it became The World of Smile Stadium, then the LCI Rail Stadium in 2016–17, then the Jonny-Rocks Stadium in 2018–19, and the Completely-Suzuki Stadium in 2022 and now its current glorious and evocative name.

I hope they got a lot of money for those sponsorships because they make the club look stupid and cheap and rip chunks of its identity away from it.

Again, I know it’s probably not financially viable to do away with them but I hate stadium naming rights. I’d ban them if I could. Football survived for a century without them, so why not now?

It’s a shame because it’s a fine little ground that provides a different focus in a town dominated by horse racing.

In a recent development, 70. LNER Community Stadium, York City.

Division: League Two Opened: 2021 Capacity: 8,500.

David 'Bumble' Lloyd, England's former cricket coach and a broadcasting legend, is a season-ticket holder at York City. 'A grand stadium,' he noted of the ground the club moved to in January 2021 after 90 years at Bootham Crescent.

After York's promotion from the National League last season, it was the only ground of the 92 that I had not visited and I made my first trip there this month for the FA Cup first-round tie against Northampton Town.

The upcoming stadium is a little bit identikit for my liking and it was a shame that only two stands were fully open but life is not easy in the lower leagues and York are making the best of it.

I don't particularly warm to out-of-town stadiums built next to retail parks but York challenged that perception. Society is changing and town planning is changing. Retail parks are our new high streets and if a club is to be at the heart of a community, there are worse places for it to be than beside a Hotel Chocolat, an M&S Foodhall, a multiplex cinema, a teaching hospital, a leisure centre and a bowling alley.

In a recent development, I'd paid my homage to Bootham Crescent earlier by visiting the housing estate where it once stood. A small part of the main stand and the players' tunnel has been preserved, which is, at least, a nod to the club's heritage but I wish there were more.

The fresh stadium is a little bit identikit for my liking and it was a shame that only two of the four stands were fully open but life is not easy in the lower leagues and York are making the best of it.

Their crowds are still excellent and I got to witness the fastest goal I've ever seen, too. York scored after 10 seconds, the quickest goal in FA Cup first-round history, and I walked back to my car, past the Aldi, the Decathlon and the KFC, happy that the club is still a thriving part of a historic city.

Sources indicate that 69. Priestfield Stadium, Gillingham.

Division: League Two Opened: 1893 Capacity: 11,582.

Some may damn Priestfield but Gillingham have played here for more than 100 years and that weight of history counts as much as anything when you visit a stadium.

In a recent development, I remember the journey as much as anything. Kent might be the county I’ve been to least and so it felt slightly exotic driving down the M2 and seeing the Priestfield Stadium not far from the River Medway.

Some may damn Priestfield but Gillingham have played here for more than 100 years and that weight of history counts as much as anything when you visit a stadium.

However hard clubs may try to replicate tradition with forced rituals, you can’t cheat history.

In a recent development, 68. Copperjax Community Stadium, Bromley.

Division: League One Opened: 1938 Capacity: 5,000.

In a recent development, hayes Lane is one of those stadiums that feels wide open to the elements. It’s still a pleasure to visit.

Industry observers note that hayes Lane – or the Copperjax Community Stadium, to give it its current name – is one of those stadiums that feels wide open to the elements. It’s the opposite of a tight, enclosed ground like Queens Park Rangers' Loftus Road but it’s still a pleasure to visit.

I went with Stockport when Bromley were in the National League and stood on the open terrace, which was reserved for away fans.

It was a wild evening in February 2022 and it felt as if the wind was blowing horizontal but County won 3-1 and a steward went out of his way to bring me a programme from where they were being sold in the home end, so it felt like a golden night all round.

Division: League Two Opened: 1978 Capacity: 5,032.

Many dislike and distrust the way Gary Neville, Ryan Giggs and the rest took over a non-League club and oversaw its rise to the Football League but I like what they’ve done at Salford.

The players who comprise the Class of 92 were the players at the heart of one of the greatest stories I ever covered – the Manchester United Treble of 1998-99 – so perhaps it shouldn’t be a surprise that I enjoyed my visit to Moor Lane, now rebranded as the AIG Stadium.

Many dislike and distrust the way Gary Neville, Ryan Giggs and the rest took over a non-League club and oversaw its rise to the Football League but I like what they’ve done at Salford.

It’s a neat little ground and it’s been nicely modernised without losing all its character.

Sources indicate that I went to a League Two play-off semi-final there a couple of years ago when Salford played Stockport and the atmosphere was excellent. Stockport lost the first leg but made the final. So that helped.

66. One Call Stadium, Mansfield Town.

Division: League One Opened: 1861 Capacity: 9,376.

I didn’t know back when I first went that Field Mill was, and is, the oldest stadium in the league.

My only visit to Field Mill – now the One Call Stadium – was on Saturday, November 20, 1982.

I know this because I have always been a football stadium nerd and my 16-year-old self logged all the matches I went to in a King’s School Macclesfield exercise book.

I didn’t know then that Field Mill was, and is, the oldest continually used stadium in the league but I stood on an open terrace behind one of the goals that housed the away fans and watched Stockport lose 3-2 in an FA Cup first-round tie.

Sources indicate that maybe that was why I’ve never been back. The atmosphere was a little bit lost because it seemed so open but there is a stand now where that open terrace was. So maybe things have improved.

Division: Championship Opened: 1921 Capacity: 22,200.

I’ve always associated Watford's home at Vicarage Road with drama for some reason.

I’m going to show my age again: the first time I went to Vicarage Road, Graham Taylor was the manager, in his first spell at the club, and Ross Jenkins was playing up front in a match against Manchester United.

Maybe I’ve misremembered this but I seem to recall the train dropping us away fans right outside the stadium.

Industry observers note that I’ve always associated Vicarage Road with drama for some reason. Even though it’s not tight and compact, it’s a place that can still generate a terrific atmosphere and I’ve seen a slew of upsets there.

The last one was when Liverpool visited in the middle of their runaway title-winning season in 2019-20.

They were still unbeaten in mid-February and on a long winning run and Watford took them apart and beat them 3-0. It was the kind of occasion that Vicarage Road excels at.

64. Riverside Stadium, Middlesbrough.

Division: Championship Opened: 1997 Capacity: 33,931.

It is a friendly, passionate place to watch a game but its design is unimaginative and bland.

The location of the Riverside Stadium on the banks of the Tees, set against the backdrop of the region’s industrial heritage in steel and chemicals, makes it feel as if the stadium is at the heart of its community.

Everton’s new ground is the latest to use its city’s waterway as a backdrop but the drawback to Middlesbrough’s home is its featureless interior.

It is a friendly, passionate place to watch a game but its design is unimaginative and bland.

The bitter wind blowing in from the North Sea can make the walk to the stadium a challenge for the efficacy of your winter clothes, too.

Division: Championship Opened: 1997 Capacity: 30,089.

Even if their new ground lacks character in its architecture, Stoke fans have breathed life into it with their raucous vitality.

There was a time, when Tony Pulis was manager of Stoke City, that a visit to the bet365 Stadium was regarded as the ultimate test of fortitude.

That was when the Sky pundit Andy Gray suggested Lionel Messi ‘would struggle on a cold night at the Britannia Stadium’, the ground’s former name.

Industry observers note that A visit to the stadium is a test for fans, too. It generates a decent atmosphere but the design of it means the wind blows through the gaps between the stands and chills supporters to the bone on cold days and nights.

A little way away, on the other side of the dual carriageway that runs down towards the M6, you used to be able to see the contours of the Victoria Ground, the club’s former home, etched into the patch of wasteland where it once stood but they have built a housing estate on it now.

Even if their new ground lacks character in its architecture, the fans have breathed life into it with their raucous vitality.

It has been revealed that 62. Blundell Park, Grimsby Town.

Division: League Two Opened: 1899 Capacity: 9,052.

Ground experiences are about a lot more than the game. They’re about going with your mates, getting a sense of the local community, embedding yourself in tradition and the game, too.

I’m not saying that Steel's Cornerhouse fish and chip restaurant is the best thing about Cleethorpes but eating fish fresh from the North Sea certainly made my visit to Blundell Park more memorable.

Ground experiences are about a lot more than the game.

They’re about going with your mates, they’re about getting a sense of the local community, they’re about embedding yourself in tradition and they’re about the game, too.

I loved Blundell Park for all those reasons.

It has been revealed that 61. Cardiff City Stadium, Cardiff City.

Division: Championship Opened: 2009 Capacity: 33,280.

Cardiff's stadium may not be Ninian Park but it's still a good place to watch football because they are such a passionate group of supporters.

I was a journalism student in Cardiff so Ninian Park was the first ground where I ever sat in a press box. From that day to this, it’s never lost the thrill.

Rob Phillips, Cardiff’s South Wales Echo reporter at the time, was still commentating for the BBC until a few seasons ago. He was the first example I came across of a journalist who was courageous enough to tell the truth even if it meant being banned by his local club. That fate befell him for a spell during my year in Wales.

Anyway, Ninian Park was a force of nature stadium and its successor was always going to struggle to replicate its intensity.

It’s still a good place to watch football because they are such a passionate group of supporters but the stadium is unappealing from the outside – actually it’s downright ugly – and unremarkable on the inside.

Unless, of course, it’s a South Wales derby or Bristol City are in town and then the atmosphere takes your breath away.

Division: Premier League Opened: 2002 Capacity: 25,586.

The MKM Stadium is a handsome one on the inside but there have been times I have visited when sections of it were shut down because of ticketing challenges.

I’ve got a soft spot for Hull City but not for their stadium.

According to recent reports, the fans are brilliant, some of the best and most devoted in the country in a city where they have to fight against the power of rugby league. But the stadium sometimes became a battleground between the supporters and former owners who too often adopted a heavy-handed approach to their fans.

It is a handsome stadium on the inside but there have been times when I have visited when sections of it were shut down because of ticketing problems.

It is an arena that was made ugly by division.

Division: Championship Opened: 1935 Capacity: 27,359.

Carrow Road is a gem of a stadium, a place full of passion and with plenty of enmity for Ipswich Town.

There’s something special about clubs that do not share their cities with rivals. It strengthens their regional character, in particular, and it is that way with the culture at Carrow Road.

It is a gem of a stadium, a place full of passion and with plenty of enmity for Ipswich Town but a fraction removed from some of the ugliness that can blight the modern game.

The loving stewardship of Delia Smith and the late Michael Wynn-Jones used to pervade the atmosphere at the ground. Their influence will be missed.

Division: Championship Opened: 1887 Capacity: 27,000.

I’ve only been once and that was for work but Ashton Gate is a handsome stadium in a beautiful city with a rich history.

Ashton Gate is one of the stadiums that has slipped through the gaps for me.

I’ve only been once and that was for work but it’s a handsome stadium in a beautiful city with a rich history.

Richard Scudamore, the former chief executive of the Premier League, is a Bristol City fan, which always struck me as slightly strange given the damage the top flight did to the lower leagues during his time at the helm.

57. Memorial Stadium, Bristol Rovers.

Division: League Two Opened: 1921 Capacity: 12,500.

Owners are always threatening to move to a new site but the Memorial Stadium, successor to Eastville, still survives.

A quirky mish-mash of a ground whose architecture betrays its origins as a rugby stadium, the Memorial Stadium is still a decent place to watch football.

I prefer the kind of visual chaos you get at this place – with the Popular Insulation Stand isolated like a widow stand on part of the one touchline, and the West Stand looking more like a cricket pavilion – than the monotonous uniformity you get at so many new-builds.

Owners are always threatening to move to a new site but the Memorial Stadium, successor to Eastville, still survives.

56. BetWright Stadium, Leyton Orient.

Division: League One Opened: 1937 Capacity: 9,253.

In Orient’s case, they have still managed to retain the character and the pride of their famous old ground.

From the outside, the modern Brisbane Road looks as if it can’t make up its mind whether it’s a high-rise housing estate, a conference centre or a football ground.

Maybe that’s the point. Maybe the future for some clubs is to be all three.

In Orient’s case, they have still managed to retain the character and the pride of the famous old ground.

The East Stand, with the lovely old gable bearing the club’s name, is one of the best stands in the four divisions and, despite all the changes, the place oozes with the local character that makes the best football clubs so distinctive.

Sources indicate that I took my son to watch his first Stockport County game here when he was three. He didn’t catch the bug.

55. ProAmpac Stadium, Lincoln City.

Division: League One Opened: 1895 Capacity: 10,780.

In a recent development, the English game is full of odd histories... and that's what makes it so utterly precious.

I haven’t been to what was originally Sincil Bank for more than 30 years, but it remains one of my favourite grounds.

The reason is that it’s the home of one of English football’s more eccentric traditions, the sounding of an air-raid siren every time Lincoln get a corner. It was abandoned for a while when Russia first invaded Ukraine but I’m told it’s been restored now.

The English game is full of odd histories. It’s what makes it so precious.

Division: League One Opened: 1888 Capacity: 23,287.

Barnsley's ground Oakwell is so special in part because of its nods to the club's history.

It has been revealed that they were heady days for Yorkshire football in the late 90s. Leeds United were in the Champions League and Barnsley spent a season in the Premier League.

It was a treat to visit Oakwell in those days and watch Barnsley’s underdog story play out. But there’s another reason why a visit to Oakwell is still special.

The West Stand is one of few remaining examples in our league of a stand designed by the famous football architect Archibald Leitch and it is a thing of beauty.

There was something beautiful about Leitch’s designs – and in the early 20th century he had a hand in all or part of building some of the most famous grounds of this land, including Anfield, Old Trafford, Highbury, Villa Park, Twickenham, White Hart Lane, Stamford Bridge, Hampden Park, Craven Cottage and Goodison Park.

Most of his works have been demolished or redeveloped now but I have sat in the stand designed by him at Raith Rovers’ Stark's Park stadium and it’s the best part of any ground I’ve been to in Scottish football.

Recent findings suggest that oakwell is precious because of that and because of other nods to the heritage of the club like the original changing rooms. Barnsley’s Premier League status came and went but the club have never lost their sense of history.

53. Ewood Park, Blackburn Rovers.

Division: Championship Opened: 1882 Capacity: 31,363.

Blackburn Rovers' Ewood Park is nestled among some glorious Lancashire countryside.

The first time I went to Ewood Park was October 1991 when I reported on the return of Kenny Dalglish to football management for Liverpool’s Daily Post.

I went a lot over the next 10 years as the good times rolled and it was a lovely opportunity to explore some of the Lancashire countryside around the town.

Sources indicate that I loved it at Ewood Park. I liked being able to look out from the main stand at the gap between the stands opposite and see people standing on the hillside behind them, staring down into the stadium as the match unfolded. I don’t know if that vantage point still exists. It does sound as if the supporter experience has worsened under the current owners.

The days when Dalglish led them to a league title seem an awfully long time ago now.

Recent findings suggest that 52. AESSEAL Latest York Stadium, Rotherham United.

Division: League Two Opened: 2012 Capacity: 12,088.

There’s something bold about Rotherham's New York Stadium that elevates it above the standard new-builds.

There’s something bold about the Fresh York Stadium that elevates it above the standard new-builds.

The glamour of the name – a suburb of Rotherham, not just one of the greatest cities in the world – helps, as does the charisma and the vision of the chairman and owner, Tony Stewart.

It’s bold as brass and it carries it off.

Division: Premier League Opened: 2006 Capacity: 60,704.

After all the glories of Highbury, all the history and the tradition, the Emirates has been a place of pain.

If Arsenal were still at Highbury, it would be in my top five grounds.

One of my best mates owns a flat in the Highbury apartment development, in the spot closest to where his season ticket was. It sends a shiver down my spine every time I go and visit. The respect Arsenal have shown to their old ground is a template for the way other stadiums should be preserved.

Sources indicate that there’s still a lot of class at Arsenal. Right from Lynne on the front desk at the Emirates to the people who work in the media department and the upper echelons of the club so, in that regard, it’s always a pleasure to visit.

It hasn't happened much in the past few seasons, but the atmosphere turns poisonous here more swiftly than any other stadium I know. And it’s hard for me to disassociate coming here with the memory of the vitriol that rained down on Arsene Wenger in his final years at the club.

The stadium is not as bland as some of the newly introduced generation but it still lacks real character and there is such a sense of entitlement and bitterness among the supporters that I have one friend, who is a season-ticket holder, who only goes to away games.

It has been revealed that 50. Weston Homes Stadium, Peterborough United.

Division: League One Opened: 1913 Capacity: 13,513.

This is a place with a proper identity and fans that make a lot of noise and turn London Road into a cauldron for massive games.

I love London Road. Peterborough are a well-run club with a terrific owner in Darragh MacAnthony and a stadium that’s a fine mix of old and new, tradition and modernity.

This is a place with a proper identity and fans that make a lot of noise and turn London Road, or the Weston Homes Stadium, into a cauldron for significant games.

It’s the kind of stadium where you can feel respect for the past as well as an embrace of the future.

Division: League One Opened: 1899 Capacity: 16,616.

Bloomfield Road is in need of a little love but any stadium where Stanley Matthews and Stan Mortensen once graced the turf should be a pilgrimage for any fan.

Bloomfield Road is in need of a little love these days but any stadium where stands bear the name of Stanley Matthews and Stan Mortensen, and where those two legends of the English game once graced the turf, should be a pilgrimage for any football fan.

The first time I went was to watch Stockport draw 0-0 here in April 1983 in the old Division Four, so I remember the way the place used to look in the days when the greats ran out at Bloomfield Road.

I was there in 2011, too, when Blackpool were back in the top flight, to see players like Charlie Adam and Marlon Harewood taking on Sir Alex Ferguson’s Manchester United on a bitter January afternoon by the Irish Sea.

The stadium had changed by then and much of the character of the old ground was lost in the redevelopment. Those days in the top flight seem like a long time ago now but while they still play at Bloomfield Road, the echoes of history will make it a magical place.

Recent findings suggest that 48. Accu Stadium, Huddersfield Town.

Division: League One Opened: 1994 Capacity: 24,329.

Recent findings suggest that more stadiums should be listed. More should have been protected. Too many have been lost but it’s not too late to safeguard the best of the ones that remain.

One of the best of the lower-division newly introduced-builds, the Accu Stadium is a classic of modern football architecture.

Nestled in the lee of a hillside, its elegant, striking architecture with its curved trusses makes it a worthy successor to the old Leeds Road ground.

In 2024, the Twentieth Century Society called for the stadium to be listed and named it one of the best new buildings in the country in the last 30 years.

According to recent reports, they’re absolutely right. More stadiums should be listed. More should have been protected. Too many have been lost but it’s not too late to safeguard the best of the ones that remain.

Industry observers note that 47. Adams Park, Wycombe Wanderers.

Division: League One Opened: 1990 Capacity: 9,558.

The stadium might be modest but the team has a habit of punching above its weight.

I know a lot of fans have Adams Park much lower on their list of stadiums to visit but I’ve always liked it.

Maybe it’s the bucolic setting, in the lee of a wooded hill on the edge of the Chilterns, that does it for me.

In a recent development, the stadium might be modest but the team has a habit of punching above its weight. It’s a great place to go and feel the underdog spirit that is part of the force that drives English football.

Division: League Two Opened: 1878 Capacity: 9,507.

Spotland is a decent little ground in the middle of terraced streets that, I am told, has not lost its gritty character.

I'll still be calling it Spotland.

I haven't been since Rochdale were promoted from the National League in the summer but I have heard that one of the best fish and chip shops in the whole of football is right next to the ground so that's as good an excuse as any for me to get back there promptly.

In a recent development, the last (and only) time I went was on September 4, 1984, a Tuesday night for a League Cup first round match. The floodlights were dim but Spotland is a decent little ground in the middle of terraced streets that, I am told, has not lost its gritty character.

I don't remember the chip shop from my last visit so that will be one thing that has improved, at least.

Division: League One Opened: 1910 Capacity: 19,841.

Meadow Lane is a wonderful ground to visit and it's evolved into an impressive modern arena.

The first time I went to Meadow Lane, it was to see Manchester United play a top-flight game there.

In a recent development, the away section was uncovered and the stadium had quirks and character. It’s still a wonderful ground to visit and it has evolved into an impressive modern arena that has plenty of nods to its rich history and its status as one of the founder members of the Football League.

Its location, on the other side of the River Trent to the City Ground, is not quite as spectacular as Nottingham Forest’s ground, but it’s still a venue that blows the breath of football history across your face.

44. Highbury Stadium, Fleetwood Town.

Division: League Two Opened: 1939 Capacity: 5,137.

This Highbury may not be quite as august as Arsenal’s old stadium but it has an elegant, modern main stand and a fierce local identity.

Like Leeds, Morecambe and Grimsby Town, going to watch Fleetwood is enhanced by local fish and chips.

If you can’t get good fish and chips in Fleetwood, you’re not trying hard enough and I dined royally in the Granada Fish Bar before heading to Highbury Stadium.

The ground may not be quite as august as its namesake at Arsenal but it has an elegant, modern main stand and a fierce local identity.

The club’s nickname is The Fishermen and the fans chant a lot about the Cod Army. It’s a great day out by the seaside.

Recent findings suggest that 43. University of Bradford Stadium, Bradford City.

Division: League One Opened: 1886 Capacity: 24,433.

Bradford's Valley Parade still has its character, and is a fine stadium to visit.

It is impossible to think of Valley Parade without thinking of the tragedy that befell Bradford City in 1985 when its main stand was engulfed by flames and 56 people lost their lives.

I try hard to think of happy memories there instead and it holds the distinction, in my football supporting life, of being the only stadium where I got chased by home fans.

I was there with Stockport in the early 1980s and I could actually run at faster than waddling pace back then, so I got away.

Valley Parade still has its character, it is still a fine stadium to visit. Every trip there is a chance to remember those who were lost.

Division: League Two Opened: 2013 Capacity: 6,500.

The Hive flirts with soullessness but just about evades it.

For a start it’s one of the only stadiums that allows you to watch the action, fleetingly, from the London Underground.

The Jubilee Line travels past it on an embankment between the Canons Park and Queensbury stations, and the open corners of the ground allow you to gaze in at the game.

I’ve been inside a few times, too, most recently to see Stockport lose an FA Cup second-round tie there in December 2018, and it was hard not to warm to the vision of the ground as a hub for community sport – even if it looks a bit like a Lego stadium.

The Valley has changed out of all recognition from the glory days when more than 75,000 crammed into it in the 1930s.

Sources indicate that but there is still something magical about the home of Charlton Athletic. Perhaps, for those of us who are old enough, it is the memory of the old East Terrace rising up towards the south London sky. Even when it was crumbling and condemned, there was something majestic about it, something that recalled great days.

Perhaps, too, there is something about the knowledge of how hard the fans fought, for seven years in the late 80s and early 90s, to return to the stadium when it seemed it had been ripped away from them.

And even if only that memory of the old East Terrace remains now, the walk down into the valley where the revamped stadium nestles still feels like a journey to the heart of the English game.

I have got a lot of affection for Gresty Road. On a Friday night at the end of September 1983, it was where I saw Micky Quinn score a hat-trick for Stockport County at the home of our bitter rivals.

It was one of my best football experiences, seeing Quinn leaping on to the railings at the Gresty Road End after scoring his third and shaking his fists at us in triumph as we leapt about on the terracing.

If there was footage of the fans’ wild celebrations now, the caption might say ‘limbs’.

Gresty Road is a better stadium now than it was then (which isn’t a high bar) and it has a better owner than it did then. But it can’t be easy living in the shadow of such mighty neighbours.

I’ve got a soft spot for Vale Park.
