Rainforest adaptation in late Homo erectus from southern China

📅 22 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 56 min read (11142 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Nature

⏱️ ~56 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that homo erectus represents one of the longest-persisting hominin species, with a geographic range from Africa to eastern Eurasia from approximately 1.9 million years ago1 to 108 thousand years ago (ka)2.
  • erectus finds in East and Southeast Asia represent a key part of the hominin evolutionary history of the Asian region, with China sitting in an important location to understand the dispersal, interactions and adaptations of this species6,7,8.
  • Establishing the environmental context of H.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that homo erectus represents one of the longest-persisting hominin species, with a geographic range from Africa to eastern Eurasia from approximately 1.9 million years ago1 to 108 thousand years ago (ka)2. Despite this, there are still large gaps in our understanding of the adaptation capabilities of this species and the extent of its persistence in China. Assumptions over ecological preferences based on the Trinil3, Sangiran4 and Ngandong2 (in Java) open woodland–grassland mosaics have persisted, combined with limited direct stable carbon isotope measurements in Asia. Here we present a rich temporal and environmental context for nine hominin teeth, eight of which were morphologically and genetically identified as H. erectus5, found in two sister caves in Guangxi province, southern China. We modelled 43 radiometric ages from five dating techniques to establish a timeline for H. erectus presence in this region. Stable and clumped isotopes and trace elements from teeth were used to establish the dominant environments and their behavioural responses. We show that H. erectus was present in southern China between 324 and 184 ka, which is substantially more recent than previously established in this region for unequivocally H. erectus fossils at approximately 400 ka. The evidence suggests that they were persisting in closed rainforest ecosystems, thought to be the domain of only Homo sapiens, and were demonstrating long-term mobility and ecological flexibility. This evidence challenges the assumptions over the ecological preferences and behavioural limitations of H. erectus.

Early and late H. erectus finds in East and Southeast Asia represent a key part of the hominin evolutionary history of the Asian region, with China sitting in an important location to understand the dispersal, interactions and adaptations of this species6,7,8. There is a rich fossil record for H. erectus in China in Yuanmou (1.7 million years ago)9,10,11, Gongwangling (1.6 million years ago)12, Zhoukoudian (780–400 ka)13, Nanjing (approximately 650 ka)14 and Hexian (410 ka)15 (Supplementary Information 1). However, most of these sites are located in north and central China, with reliably identified and dated H. erectus fossils being conspicuously rare in southern China, especially during the Middle Pleistocene. This makes it particularly challenging to establish their ecological preferences. Furthermore, evidence of younger H. erectus (less than 400 ka) is almost entirely absent from China. This temporal gap is particularly striking given that H. erectus persisted in Java until 117–108 ka at Ngandong2, raising fundamental questions about the species’ distribution, ecological adaptations and ultimate fate in mainland China.

Establishing the environmental context of H. erectus is essential for understanding the species’ ecological flexibility and adaptive capabilities. The youngest Javanese H. erectus at Ngandong2 persisted in woodland refugia as rainforests expanded across the region, raising questions about whether encroaching closed-canopy forests contributed to the species’ eventual extinction2,16. Yet, there have been very few stable isotope studies on H. erectus evidence, as the material is often limited by diagenetic alteration3. Recent work has debated whether non-H. sapiens Middle Pleistocene hominins possessed the adaptive capabilities to exploit tropical rainforest environments17,18. Studying the forested landscapes of tropical southern China during the Middle and Late Pleistocene19 thus provides a crucial test case for assessing H. erectus ecological adaptations. Furthermore, understanding mobility patterns through techniques such as strontium isotope analysis can reveal how these populations used their landscapes and how they connected with contemporaneous populations across broader regional scales20,21.

Industry observers note that since the Pleistocene, tropical forest and grassland environments in southern China have provided a critical biogeographical corridor for faunal dispersals between northern latitudes and insular Southeast Asia22,23,24. The karst landscapes and cave systems of the region have yielded abundant Pleistocene faunal assemblages, yet there is at the moment no clear evidence that H. erectus was part of the Stegodon–Ailuropoda fauna in this region6. This raises questions as to whether the absence of H. erectus in southern China, particularly during the late Middle Pleistocene, is a consequence of ecological constraints preventing H. erectus from exploiting southern China’s tropical forest environments18, representing an effective biogeographic barrier25, or results from other factors such as an imbalance in research intensity7, a reflection of real absence of the species in the region due to alternative dispersal routes through the Tibetan corridor6, the absence of secure dating data on many out-of-context teeth, the misidentification of fragmentary remains (particularly with morphologically similar Pongo teeth26), taphonomic and preservation biases in tropical environments18, lower population densities leading to reduced fossil representation27 or the occupation of an ecological niche that is not readily preserved in cave deposits18. Distinguishing between these scenarios requires well-dated, robustly identified hominin fossils with detailed environmental context—evidence that has been lacking.

Sources indicate that to provide a temporal and environmental context for the eight H. erectus teeth6 from Baxian and Naxian caves in southern China (Fig. 1, Supplementary Information 2 and 3 and Extended Data Figs. 1–3), we used five independent dating techniques to constrain the sediments: post-infrared infrared-stimulated luminescence (pIR-IRSL) dating of feldspars, optically stimulated luminescence (OSL) dating of quartz (Supplementary Information 4), uranium-series (U-series) dating of fossil teeth (Supplementary Information 5), coupled U-series–electron spin resonance (US-ESR) dating of fossil teeth (Supplementary Information 6) and U-series dating of carbonate capping flowstones (Supplementary Information 7), all integrated through the use of two Bayesian age models—ChronoModel and OxCal (Supplementary Information 8). Environmental reconstruction was achieved through faunal analysis (Supplementary Information 3), bulk and sequential stable isotope analysis of faunal and H. erectus tooth enamel (Supplementary Information 9) and clumped isotope thermometry of cave sediments (Supplementary Information 10). Finally, we assessed individual mobility patterns through laser-ablation trace element mapping and strontium isotope analysis of hominin tooth enamel, integrated with a regional strontium isoscape constructed using random forest machine learning to identify potential source regions (Supplementary Information 11). These multiple lines of evidence, replicated across laboratories in China and Australia, provide, to our knowledge, the first comprehensive temporal, environmental and behavioural context for late H. erectus in southern China.

a, The locations of China (green region on the world inset), Beijing (black dot) and the Chongzuo study area located in Guangxi Zhuang Autonomous Region province, southern China (black star). b, The location of Chongzuo city in relation to Nanning and Hanoi, illustrating the dense network of karst (tan topography) that comprises this landscape. The black dashed box marks the study region and the red square represents the cave locations. The location of the lower section of Red River valley in Vietnam (discussed in the text) is marked by a red dashed line. c, Location of the Naxian and Baxian caves (red stars) connected by a 15-km karst corridor near the meandering Zuojiang River and the city of Chongzuo. Scale bars, 100 km (b), 10 km (c). Maps adapted from ref. 19, CC BY 4.0.

Industry observers note that the Naxian and Baxian caves, located 15 km apart and situated 13 km to the northwest and 20 km to the north of Chongzuo City, respectively, are connected by a straight karst valley corridor (Fig. 1, Extended Data Fig. 1a,b,e,f and Supplementary Information 2). They are both horizontal caves at 226 and 218 m above sea level, positioned 5–7 m above the valley floor (Extended Data Fig. 2), with small fossil chambers at the rear of each cave (Fig. 2). The chambers contain remarkably similar dense, cemented, cataclastic breccias that have yielded a combined total of over 18,000 mammalian fossils, which were initially accumulated by porcupines28, including hominin remains (Supplementary Information 2). The fossil-bearing breccias (Extended Data Fig. 3) were capped by thick flowstone and underlain by younger mixed sediments (Extended Data Fig. 1d,h). This similarity suggests deposition under comparable environmental conditions.

Industry observers note that a, Cave plan for Naxian cave, showing the locations of the test pits (T1–T3) and fossil chamber at the rear of the cave. b, Expanded illustration of test pits T1 and T2 and fossil chamber in a, showing the spatial relationship between the sampling locations. c, Cross-sectional stratigraphic profile of the fossil chamber and excavation pit T2, drawn from location A–A′ in a, showing the sampling locations in the breccia, flowstone and underlying mixed unit. d,Cave plan for Baxian cave, showing the location of the two fossil chambers at the rear of the cave and the location of the test pits (T1–T3). e, Cross-sectional stratigraphic profile of the fossil chamber and excavation pit T2 drawn from location B–B′ in d, showing the sampling locations that correspond to the legend. f, Enlarged fossil chamber, showing the spatial location of the sampling in pits T2 and T3 in d. g,h, Composite stratigraphy for Naxian (g) and Baxian (h) caves, showing the sampling locations within the flowstone, breccia and underlying sandy clay. At each location, the symbols refer to the dating techniques in the legend, and the sampling codes and results have been included. Scale bars, 5 m (a), 1 m (c,e), 10 m (d).

Sources indicate that of the resulting 45 radiometric ages from both caves (Extended Data Figs. 4–7), 43 were modelled and given similar modelled age estimates (OxCal: 312–161 ka; ChronoModel: 324–184 ka at 2σ uncertainties; Extended Data Fig. 8), but the ChronoModel results were used owing to their greater outlier robustness and more reliable lower age limit. These results indicate that the age of H. erectus fossil evidence lies between 324 and 184 ka for the Baxian caves, and between 319 and 241 ka for the Naxian caves. These error limits are overlapping and broadly contemporaneous, and indicate a 95% probability that H. erectus was in this area sometime between 324 and 184 ka (see Supplementary Information 4–8 for all dating tables, data and discussion of limitations, uncertainties and choice of model; Fig. 3). The overlapping age uncertainties for the caves of approximately 78,000 years suggest a contemporaneous or near-contemporaneous presence on this landscape. The modelled ages are consistent across all five dating techniques within their respective uncertainties, providing robust constraints on the timing of H. erectus presence in this region.

Recent findings suggest that a, Stratigraphy (overlying flowstone, fossil-bearing breccia and underlying clay) and modelled age range using ChronoModel (324–184 ka) of the fossil-bearing breccia for Baxian cave. The image depicts the landscape at this time, including an enclosed rainforest, H. erectus and associated fauna. b, Stratigraphy and modelled age range (319–241 ka) for the Naxian fossil-bearing breccia, along with a reconstruction of the environment around the cave at that time. The age uncertainties for the caves overlap over a period of approximately 78,000 years (green box). These reconstructions are derived from trace element and stable isotope data from the human and faunal remains seen in c and d. The dashed lines in a and b denote the age ranges for Baxian and Naxian caves, respectively, and correspond to the length of the landscape image for each cave. c, Geographic assignment based on UnionP probability surfaces calculated for three distinct 87Sr/86Sr values measured in H. erectus—(i) 0.714, (ii) 0.719 and (iii) 0.724—showing its mobility across southern China and northern Southeast Asia. The corresponding strontium isoscape and full method are provided in Supplementary Information 11. d, Biplots of δ13Ccarbon source and δ18O values by taxon in relation to vegetation type. Biplot of faunal enamel δ13Ccarbon source (plant-equivalent values; ‰ Vienna Peedee Belemnite standard (VPDB)) and δ18O (‰ VPDB) at Baxian (top; 324–184 ka) and Naxian (bottom; 319–241 ka) caves. Each taxon is represented by a unique combination of colour and shape. Shaded background areas indicate ecological zones: dense-canopy forest (green shading), C3 vegetation (light green shading) and C4 grassland (yellow shading). The unshaded interval between C3 and C4 represents the C3–C4 intermediate zone. This framework allows direct comparison of faunal isotopic signatures against expected vegetation regimes. A large proportion of taxa from both sites fall within the dense-canopy forest zone, supporting the interpretation of closed-canopy rainforest environments. Scale bars, 50 km (c). Bax, Baxian; Nax, Naxian.

The faunal assemblages from the Baxian and Naxian caves are taxonomically diverse and remarkably similar in composition (Supplementary Information 3 and Extended Data Fig. 3). Both assemblages include numerous taxa that have since become locally extinct, including Pongo, Elephas and rhinoceros Dicerorhinus, though most remain extant elsewhere in Asia. Notably, H. erectus, Stegodon and ‘Megalovis’ are globally extinct. Habitat preference analysis indicates that both assemblages are strongly dominated by forest-dwelling taxa (Supplementary Fig. 3), which is consistent with predominantly forested landscapes during the time of deposition.

In a recent development, the plant-equivalent stable carbon isotope values for the Baxian faunal teeth, after correction for species-specific diet-to-enamel enrichment factors based on body mass29 (Supplementary Information 9), range from −31.5 to −23.0‰ (average = −27.6 ± 1.87‰ (1σ)), while lower values observed at the Naxian cave range from −34.0 to −25.1‰ (average = −29.4 ± 2.45‰ (1σ)). Both assemblages yield values well below the dense-canopy forest threshold of −27.5‰ (ref. 28), with no evidence of C4 plant consumption or even C3–C4 intermediate signatures (Fig. 3 and Extended Data Fig. 9). These data indicate that the fauna at both sites derived their dietary carbon exclusively from C3 vegetation, with the frequency of canopy-related values exceeding those reported for equatorial African rainforest systems29 and being comparable to that documented for western Amazonian forests30,31,32. This pattern is particularly notable given that several of the taxa represented in the assemblages are known elsewhere to exploit mixed C3–C4 resources or to incorporate substantial C4-derived inputs into their diets in more open environments16.

Independent oxygen isotope (δ18O) and clumped isotope (Δ47) analyses further support these environmental reconstructions, indicating humid tropical conditions with higher precipitation and cooler temperatures than modern values in this region (Extended Data Fig. 9 and Supplementary Information 9 and 10).

In a recent development, three H. erectus teeth from the Naxian cave (NX-B1, NX-B2 and NX-A1) show similarly low isotopic values, with carbon values ranging from −15.0 to −14.0‰, which fall at the boundary between dense-canopy forest and more open C3 vegetation. Although the dataset is limited (n = 3) and presently restricted to the Naxian locality, these values are fully consistent with those observed across the much larger faunal assemblage and fall within the range expected for consumers deriving their dietary carbon from closed-canopy C3 vegetation, demonstrating that these late H. erectus populations exploited tropical rainforest resources.

Industry observers note that high-resolution trace element mapping on one H. erectus individual from the Baxian cave (PA1799) yielded 87Sr/86Sr ratios ranging from 0.7110 to 0.7220 (Supplementary Information 11 and Extended Data Fig. 10), while three H. erectus teeth sampled from the Naxian cave demonstrated overlapping but distinct ranges. All four individuals indicate either movement between geologically distinct regions or consumption of resources from multiple locations during childhood (2–6 years), corresponding to the period of tooth formation.

It has been revealed that A regional strontium isoscape for southern China and northern Southeast Asia33 (Supplementary Information 11) reveals substantial spatial heterogeneity in predicted 87Sr/86Sr ratios, with the local Baxian–Naxian region characterized by relatively homogeneous values (0.710–0.715), reflecting the dominant Carboniferous–Permian limestone karst geology (Fig. 3 and Extended Data Fig. 10). More radiogenic signatures (0.717–0.723) occur to the west and northwest in mountainous areas underlain by Precambrian and Palaeozoic metamorphic rocks, while intermediate to more radiogenic values (0.715–0.720) characterize regions to the south, including the Red River valley of northern Vietnam.

According to recent reports, geographic assignment probability maps generated for three representative 87Sr/86Sr values observed in the human tooth profiles indicate that these H. erectus individuals may have moved between the local limestone karst regions and more distant areas during childhood, with the most radiogenic signatures potentially pointing towards areas as far afield as northern Vietnam, which connect southern China with mainland Southeast Asia (Figs. 1 and 3 and Extended Data Fig. 10).

Recent findings suggest that our results demonstrate that H. erectus was present in southern China between 324 and 184 ka (Fig. 3 and Extended Data Fig. 8), representing, to our knowledge, the youngest reliably dated occurrence of this species in China and the first with robust chronological constraints from southern China. The integration of multiple independent dating techniques combined with Bayesian age modelling provides unprecedented temporal resolution for late H. erectus in mainland Asia. These findings fundamentally alter our understanding of the species’ persistence and distribution in China, extending the documented record by more than 200,000 years beyond the previous youngest occurrences in Hexian and Nanjing14,15, and establishing southern China as a key region for late-surviving populations during the late Middle Pleistocene (for example, ref. 19).

According to recent reports, the temporal importance of this discovery extends beyond simply filling a chronological gap. The age uncertainty range of 324–184 ka places these H. erectus populations at some point within marine isotope stages 9 through 6, raising intriguing questions about potential contemporaneity or overlap with Homo longi (Denisovans) identified in Cobra cave (Laos)34, Baishiya cave (Tibetan Plateau)35, Harbin (northeast China)36,37,38 and the Penghu Channel off the western shore of Taiwan39. The temporal proximity of these various hominin populations across China during the late Middle Pleistocene suggests a more complex biogeographical landscape than previously recognized, with multiple hominin lineages potentially coexisting across different ecological zones and elevational gradients.

In a recent development, moreover, the environmental context revealed by our multi-proxy analyses challenges prevailing assumptions about late H. erectus ecological constraints and mobility patterns. The combined evidence demonstrates unequivocally that these late H. erectus populations exploited closed-canopy tropical rainforest environments and may have conducted long-distance movement beyond the local karst terrain during childhood. The ecological implications of this rainforest use and mobility are profound. Archaeological evidence has so far suggested that H. sapiens was the only member of our genus to specialize in the regular exploitation of these environments18, as early as 150 ka in western Africa40,41. In Southeast Asia, recent isotopic observations of declines in C4 environments and expansion of rainforest in the Middle to early Late Pleistocene have been associated with the disappearance of non-H. sapiens hominin taxa42,43, seemingly unable to shift from mixed savannah–woodland habitats to these increasingly closed forests16,44. However, our data directly challenge this view by demonstrating that H. erectus was not ecologically excluded from rainforest environments (Fig. 3) and that long-distance mobility into these environments may have been a common behavioural pattern rather than exceptional behaviour by isolated individuals.

These findings contrast markedly with Early and Middle Pleistocene H. erectus occupations at Trinil3 and Sangiran in Java4 (Extended Data Fig. 9b). The youngest Javanese H. erectus at Ngandong2 persisted in relatively open woodland refugia2, leading to suggestions that expanding rainforests may have contributed to the species’ eventual extinction in Java2,16. Among early hominin-bearing sites in East and Southeast Asia (Extended Data Fig. 9b), the Naxian and Baxian cave results most closely resemble those from Lida Ajer, Sumatra (73–63 ka), an early H. sapiens site also characterized by closed-canopy rainforest45. This demonstrates that H. erectus was, at minimum, capable of persisting among rainforest fauna, even if such habitats did not represent its optimal ecological niche.

Areas in northern Vietnam, such as the Red River valley (Figs. 1 and 3), have long been recognized as a critical biogeographical corridor connecting the karst uplands of southern China with the lowlands of mainland Southeast Asia24. The limited strontium isotope evidence tentatively suggests that late H. erectus populations may have been utilizing similar corridors for seasonal movements, long-distance migrations or resource procurement. This large range (potentially around 250 km) through mostly enclosed environments challenges assumptions about the limited ranging behaviour of H. erectus and suggests behavioural sophistication in landscape use.

It has been revealed that our findings collectively demonstrate that late Middle Pleistocene H. erectus was present in southern China, surviving contemporaneously with H. longi and exhibiting considerable ecological and behavioural flexibility. Rather than being restricted to open savanna or woodland habitats, as traditionally assumed, these populations persisted in closed-canopy tropical rainforests while simultaneously engaging in potential long-distance mobility across diverse ecological and geological landscapes. This evidence challenges the characterization of H. erectus as a species unable to exploit complex tropical forest environments. Whether these adaptations were specific to the late-surviving populations in southern China alone remains to be seen, but further stable isotope work on other Middle Pleistocene sites is vital to address this question. However, the presence of morphologically and genetically confirmed H. erectus in southern China between 324 and 184 ka, combined with the environmental and suggested mobility evidence, is sufficient to necessitate a re-evaluation of the species’ adaptive capabilities, biogeographical range and ultimate fate in mainland Asia.

The caves were discovered using local knowledge and targeted reconnaissance hunting for breccia in the rear chambers. The locations of test pits within the caves were selected on the basis of these reconnaissance surveys. Excavation grids were based on the shape of cave passages and distribution of fossil-rich deposits. Jackhammers were used to break blocks of fossil breccia, and the fossils were extracted using geological hammers. Fine cleaning, identification and cataloguing were conducted in the laboratories at Shandong University and the Institute of Vertebrate Palaeontology and Palaeoanthropology (IVPP).

The fossil-bearing breccia and associated sediments from the fossil chambers of both caves were sampled in situ under subdued red-light conditions (Fig. 2a,d) and were processed using standard sample purification procedures for quartz and feldspar separation including a 40% and 10% wash in hydrofluoric acid for 45 and 10 mins, respectively46. Single aliquots of 90–125 µm feldspar and 180–212 µm quartz or feldspar grains were processed in a Riso TL-DA-20 equipped with an automated DASH set-up, a dual-laser single-grain attachment47 and a blue- and ultraviolet-sensitive Electron Tube photo-multiplier tube (PDM9107Q-AP-TTL-03), using either a blue filter pack (Schott BG-39, 2 mm, and Corning 7-59, 4 mm) for feldspars or U340 filters (2 × Hoya U340, 3.5 mm) for quartz. Data were collected using Sequence Pro v.4.65 and analysed in Analyst v.4.57, DRAC v.1.3 and on spreadsheets designed in Microsoft Excel 365 v.2607. Feldspar equivalent doses were corrected according to the results of the anomalous fading tests (using a weighted mean fading rate of 2.0 ± 0.2% per decade)48, but no residual corrections were undertaken, and the equivalent doses for both feldspar and quartz were then run through either a central age model for the single-aliquot results or a minimum age model49 to identify the single-grain population that experienced the most bleaching before burial. All luminescence analysis was conducted at the ‘Traps’ luminescence dating facility at Macquarie University in Sydney, Australia.

In a recent development, measurements of 238U, 235U, 232Th and 40K were estimated using Geiger–Muller multi-counter beta counting and thick-source alpha counting of dried and powdered sediment samples in the laboratory, combined with in situ gamma spectrometry in the field. The corresponding (dry) beta and gamma dose rates were obtained using the conversion factors in ref. 50 and the beta-dose attenuation factors in ref. 51. Cosmic-ray dose rates were estimated from previously published relationships52, making allowance for the sediment overburden at the sample locality (ranging from 3.99 to 0.20 m), the altitude (ranging from 2,000 to 176 m above sea level) and geomagnetic latitude and longitude of the sampling sites.

Seven H. erectus teeth from the Naxian (n = 6) and Baxian (n = 1) caves were analysed for U-series dating across two laboratories in China and Australia. U-series measurements were undertaken using a laser-ablation multi-collector inductively coupled plasma mass spectrometer (MC-ICP-MS) at the Geoarchaeology and Archaeometry Research Group (GARG), Southern Cross University, according to protocols in ref. 53 and in a Neptune MC-ICP-MS at the School of Geography Science, Nanjing Normal University according to refs. 54,55. Laser ablation (at Southern Cross University) was performed with a Fresh Wave Research 213 nm laser, and thorium (230Th, 232Th) and uranium (234U, 235U, 238U) isotopes were measured on a Thermo Neptune XT MC-ICP-MS. Teeth were ablated using rasters of 5 min each and were measured with standards before and after. Uranium and thorium were separated using conventional anion-exchange chromatography at Nanjing, and the U–Th solution was then introduced into the MC-ICP-MS via a DSN-100 desolvation nebulizer system. Isotopic ratios were measured using a detector configuration that allows for the simultaneous measurement of U and Th isotopes56,57.

One H. erectus tooth and one Pongo tooth from the Baxian cave (n = 2) were selected for coupled ESR and U-series dating at GARG, Southern Cross University. Enamel fragments from each tooth were separated using a hand-held diamond saw following the protocol developed in ref. 58. Fragments were then measured at room temperature on a Freiberg MS5000 ESR X-band spectrometer at a modulation amplitude of 0.1 mT, 10 scans, 2 mW power, 100 G sweep and 100 kHz modulation frequency. Each fragment was irradiated, following exponentially increasing irradiation times. Sediment elemental concentrations, external beta and gamma dose rate contributions, and water content were obtained from in situ measurements. The external beta-dose rates have been extrapolated from the U, Th and K contents measured on a portion of sediment sub-sample (approximately 8 g). The external gamma dose rates were determined in situ using a portable gamma spectrometer at each site. The equivalent doses were estimated using Matlab-based MCdose software v.2.0.

Separate sub-samples were hand-drilled from the fresh cross-section of the in situ capping flowstones from Naxian and Baxian caves and processed at the Radiogenic Isotope Facility, University of Queensland (n = 6), and six soda straws and one sample of secondary calcite cement were processed at the School of Geography Science, Nanjing Normal University (n = 7). The powdered sub-samples were subjected to chemical treatment and isotopic measurements by mass spectrometry56. U-series dating of the speleothem samples were conducted at the University of Queensland using a Nu Plasma MC-ICP-MS, and analytical procedures followed previous publications for MC-ICP-MS57,58,59. The 230Th/234U ages were calculated using Isoplot EX 3.75 (ref. 60) and half-lives of 75,690 years for 230Th and 245,250 years for 234U (ref. 61). U-series dating of the speleothem samples was carried out at Nanjing Normal University using a Neptune MC-ICP-MS. U-series ages were calculated using the half-lives of 75,584 years for 230Th and 245,620 years for 234U (ref. 62). Non-radiogenic 230Th was corrected using an assumed bulk-Earth atomic 230Th/232Th ratio of (4.4 ± 2.2) × 10−6 (refs. 54,55).

Two Bayesian modelling programs were used to analyse selected independent age estimates (n = 43) (Supplementary Information 8) and to evaluate the uncertainties associated with the combined dating techniques applied to both sites (Supplementary Tables 7–15): OxCal (v.4.4.4, available at https://c14.arch.ox.ac.uk/oxcal.html)63 and ChronoModel (v.3.2.7, https://chronomodel.com/)64. The analyses incorporated the probability distributions of individual ages, constraints imposed by stratigraphic relationships and the reported minimum or maximum nature of some of the individual age estimates. Each individual age was included as a Gaussian distribution (with mean and s.d. defined by the age estimate and their associated uncertainties), and the resulting age ranges for each phase of deposition were presented at 2σ. OxCal allows the identification of boundary ages between each layer to constrain the fossil layer and ChronoModel was applied to assess the extent to which identical or similar data could be obtained. Both modelling results have been presented for transparency.

Three H. erectus specimens from the Naxian cave, as well as 47 faunal teeth from the Baxian cave and 38 from the Naxian cave (n = 41 in total), were taxonomically identified and prepared for stable isotope analysis, following established preparation methods65 (but see refs. 66,67). The resulting δ13C and δ18O values were measured using a ThermoFisher MAT253+ in six separate measurement blocks per sample at the Earth and Environmental Sciences’ Stable Isotope Geochemistry Laboratory at the University of Queensland. The evolved CO2 gases from the Naxian teeth were analysed for carbon and oxygen isotope compositions using a Thermo Delta V Advantage isotope ratio mass spectrometer housed at the Key Laboratory of Archaeological Sciences and Technology, Shandong University. Stable isotope measurements on the three H. erectus teeth were carried out at the Service de spectrométrie de masse isotopique du Muséum national d’Histoire naturelle, Paris, and analysed using a Thermo Delta V Advantage isotope ratio mass spectrometer. To assess isotopic differences among sites, we applied non-parametric and multivariate tests. For univariate comparisons, Kruskal–Wallis tests revealed highly significant differences in both δ13Ccarbon source (χ² = 181.5, d.f. = 6, P < 0.001) and δ18O (χ² = 114.4, d.f. = 6, P < 0.001) among sites. All statistical analyses were conducted using the open-source program R software (v.4.5.1)68.

Three in situ samples were collected in bulk (CBAX2, CBAX3, CBAX4) from the breccia at Baxian and the clumped isotope analysis was undertaken in the Macquarie GeoAnalytical Stable Isotope Facility using a ThermoFisher dual-inlet MAT253+ mass spectrometer. The results were processed using the Easotope software package69. The final Δ47 value for each sample was then averaged and reported with 95% confidence intervals, before temperatures were calculated using the calibration in ref. 70 for 90 °C reactions. Using these temperatures, the oxygen isotopic composition of the precipitating fluid (δ18Ofluid) was calculated using the equation in ref. 71.

Sources indicate that one H. erectus tooth from Baxian was sectioned with a high-precision diamond saw and polished to a smoothness of greater than 5 μm. Laser ablation combined with ICP-MS was used for trace elemental mapping analyses using an ESI NWR193 coupled to an Agilent 7900 ICP-MS at GARG, Southern Cross University, according to the procedures in refs. 19,72. A laser spot size of 40 μm, a scan speed of 80 μm s−¹, a laser intensity of 60% (approximately 1 J mm−2) and a total integration time of 0.50 s were used to produce data points that corresponded to a pixel size of approximately 40 × 40 μm. NIST610 and NIST612 (certified standard reference materials) were used to assess signal drift. Strontium isotope analysis (87Sr/86Sr) was conducted on four H. erectus teeth: one from Baxian cave and three from Naxian cave, also using laser-ablation MC-ICP-MS at the GARG facility. Enamel fragments were carefully extracted from regions showing low uranium concentrations and distinct elemental signatures from the surrounding dentine according to the mapping results. To contextualize the 87Sr/86Sr values obtained and assess potential mobility patterns, a regional strontium isoscape was constructed for southern China and northern Southeast Asia. The isoscape modelling was based on random forest ensemble machine learning analyses adapted from the original script developed in ref. 33 and followed the method fully described in ref. 21.

a: Combined p-value (physical uranium uptake parameter) trajectories for enamel and dentine illustrating the relative goodness-of-fit of uranium-uptake histories over the modelled time interval. The enamel curve reveals a broader temporal sensitivity, while dentine exhibits steeper p-value responses reflecting higher susceptibility to uranium migration. b: Normalised uranium-uptake curves for enamel (red) and dentine (green) showing contrasting U-uptake kinetics, with enamel characterised by delayed uptake and dentine by more rapid early incorporation. c: Frequency distribution of modelled ages generated under the US-ESR age model, illustrating the central tendency and dispersion of the Monte-Carlo age simulations used to derive the final age estimate, d H. erectus tooth from Baxian that was dated using US-ESR techniques (Supplementary Information 6).

Industry observers note that a and b are the dating results (n = 43) as separate age estimates in kyr for the five dating techniques modelled according to Oxcal and applied to the sediments and fossils of Naxian (a) and Baxian (b) caves. Data are presented as mean values +/− SD. The techniques are colour coded according to the legend and organised into the unit in which they were sampled from – the flowstone, breccia or underlying clay. Some of the techniques represent minimum ages (such as the US ages on teeth) and contain a colour coded arrow pointing the right, while other represent maximum ages such as the pIR-IRSL single aliquot dating of feldspars and contain a colour coded arrow pointing the left. The thick black horizontal boxes with dashed lines represent the boundary ages (and errors) estimated by the modelling. The boundary ages quoted represent the upper and lower age ranges for the breccia units in both caves. c and d are the dating results (n = 43) as separate age estimates in kyr modelling according to Chronomodel for the same five dating techniques. Data are presented as mean values +/− SD. The individual sample events have been organised into three phases; breccia deposition (including fossil and sediment ages), overlying flowstone precipitation and underlying clay deposition with each phase represented by a different plot. The timescale goes from more recent on the right (50 ka written as -50000) to oldest on the left (400 ka written as -400000). For Baxian (c) we have used the age uncertainty at 2 σ (95%) of the fossil teeth dated using US-ESR (H. erectus and Pongo), resulting in an age of 324-184 ka. For Naxian (d), the fossils are all dated using US only so represent minimum ages, so instead we have used the period between the overlying flowstone (as the minimum age) and the youngest soda straw in the breccia (as the maximum age) both at 2 σ (95%) uncertainty to constrain the age of breccia deposition at 319-241 ka. The use of Chronomodel compared to Oxcal has accentuated similar events and reduced the younger age uncertainty by around 20 kyr. The overlapping uncertainty between the two caves has been used to represent a Homo erectus presence at some point between 324-184 ka.

In a recent development, a Taxon-specific δ13Ccarbon source values in relation to vegetation type. δ13Ccarbon source (plant-equivalent values; ‰ VPDB at Baxian (324-184) and Naxian (319-241 ka). Shaded background areas indicate ecological zones: dense canopy forest (dark green), C3 vegetation (light green), and C4 grassland (yellow). The unshaded interval between C3 and C4 represents the C3–C4 intermediate zone. This framework allows direct comparison of faunal isotopic signatures against expected vegetation regimes. A large proportion of taxa from both sites fall within the dense canopy forest zone, supporting the interpretation of closed-canopy rainforest environments. The H. erectus values (red stars) fall within the C3 forest domain and plot at the boundary between dense canopy forest and more open C3 vegetation. b Vegetation zone proportions at hominin-bearing sites in Southeast Asia and South China. Proportional distribution of faunal δ13Ccarbon source values assigned to vegetation zones (dense canopy C3, open C3, C3–C4 intermediate, and C4). Bars show the relative contributions of each zone across six hominin-bearing sites: Trinil4, Sangiran5, Cobra Cave34,73, Duoi U’Oi74, Lida Ajer45,75, Baxian and Naxian. Baxian and Naxian are dominated by C3 signals, with substantial contributions from dense canopy vegetation, while Trinil and Sangiran show higher proportions of intermediate and C4 values, reflecting more open habitats. Lida Ajer is strongly weighted toward dense canopy values, consistent with closed rainforest settings. Together, these results illustrate marked ecological contrasts between late H. erectus contexts in China and Javanese sites, as well as affinities between Naxian and the rainforest environment of early H. sapiens at Lida Ajer75,76,77.

a Trace element distribution maps of the Baxian H. erectus tooth. LA-ICP-MS elemental maps showing the distribution of (i) 7Li/43Ca, (ii) 88Sr/43Ca, (iii) 138Ba/43Ca, and (iv) 238U/43Ca ratios normalised to calcium across a longitudinal section of the tooth. All maps show both enamel (upper/left portion, blue-green colours) and dentine (lower/right portion, predominantly dark red). The colour scales are optimised to visualise variation within the enamel tissue. Dark red areas in the dentine for Sr, Ba, and U maps indicate significantly elevated concentrations due to post-depositional diagenetic uptake from the burial environment, rendering these tissues unsuitable for life history reconstruction. In contrast, the enamel tissue displays lower concentrations and visible banding patterns, particularly Ba/Ca, and Sr/Ca maps, which reflect biogenic signals. The U/Ca map clearly illustrates the extent of diagenetic alteration, with the highest concentrations in dentine and at the enamel-dentine junction (EDJ), demonstrating the vulnerability of dental tissues to post-depositional elemental exchange. The Li/Ca map demonstrates elevated concentrations in both tissues with distinct banding in the enamel. All measurements were obtained using LA-ICP-MS with 40 μm spot size and Ca-normalization to account for matrix effects. b Strontium isotope ratio profiles across H. erectus tooth enamel from Baxian and Naxian caves. LA-MC-ICP-MS 87Sr/86Sr ratio profiles measured along linear transects across tooth enamel from (i) BAX-1 from Baxian Cave, and (ii) NX-A1, (iii) NX-B1, and (iv) NX-B2 from Naxian Cave. The x-axis represents distance in mm along the ablation transect from the cervical region toward the cusp, corresponding to the temporal sequence of enamel formation from early to late childhood. The y-axis shows 87Sr/86Sr ratios, with variation reflecting changes in geological substrate accessed through diet and drinking water during tooth formation. All four individuals exhibit substantial intra-tooth variation in 87Sr/86Sr ratios that exceeds analytical uncertainty, indicating mobility between geologically distinct regions or consumption of resources from multiple locations during childhood. BAX-1 shows 87Sr/86Sr ratios ranging from 0.7110 to 0.7220, while the Naxian specimens display overlapping ranges: NX-A1 (0.7115-0.7165), NX-B1 (0.7095-0.7165), and NX-B2 (0.7100-0.7160). The observed variation patterns provide evidence for landscape mobility of late Middle Pleistocene H. erectus populations in southern China. c Strontium isoscape and geographic assignment probabilities for H. erectus mobility in southern China and northern Southeast Asia. (i) Regional-scale strontium isoscape showing predicted bioavailable 87Sr/86Sr ratios across southern China, northern Vietnam, northern Laos, and adjacent regions. Colours indicate 87Sr/86Sr values ranging from 0.710 (dark blue) to 0.725 (pink), with the Baxian/Naxian cave sites marked by a white dot. Major cities (Hanoi, Lào Cai, Guilin) are shown for geographic reference. (ii) Prediction uncertainty map for the regional isoscape, showing standard error of predicted 87Sr/86Sr values ranging from 0.004 (yellow, low uncertainty) to 0.016 (purple, high uncertainty). (iii) Local-scale isoscape focused on a 400 km × 400 km region centred on the Baxian/Naxian sites, with scale bar representing 50 km. (iv) Prediction uncertainty map for the local isoscape (v-vii) Geographic assignment probability maps for three representative 87Sr/86Sr values observed in H. erectus tooth enamel: (v) Seq1 = 0.714, representing average values for NX-A1 and lower values in NX-B2, showing high assignment probabilities (yellow-green) concentrated within 30-50 km of the cave sites in limestone karst terrain; (vi) Seq2 = 0.719, representing transitional values observed in multiple specimens, showing assignment probabilities extending southward ~150-250 km toward the Red River valley region; (vii) Seq3 = 0.724, representing the most radiogenic values observed (particularly in BAX-1), showing assignment probabilities concentrated in the Red River valley foothills approximately 250 km south of the caves and near Lào Cai to the west, with very low probabilities in the local cave area (dark purple). The progressive southward shift in assignment probabilities from Seq1 to Seq3 indicates long-distance mobility of late H. erectus individuals between the local karst uplands and distant regions up to 250 km away during childhood tooth formation. All isoscapes generated using random forest machine learning based on33 global bioavailable strontium database.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • By Matthew Cooper | 22 Nov 2026 00:00, Last updated: 22 Nov 2026 00:00.
  • Today's Serie A predictions include Juventus at home to Venezia, as well as title-contending Inter Milan travelling to Atalanta.
  • Set to clash in Serie A's Sunday lunchtime slot, fallen giants Juventus and promoted strugglers Venezia will meet in Turin this weekend.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

By Matthew Cooper | 22 Nov 2026 00:00, Last updated: 22 Nov 2026 00:00.

Today's Serie A predictions include Juventus at home to Venezia, as well as title-contending Inter Milan travelling to Atalanta.

Set to clash in Serie A's Sunday lunchtime slot, fallen giants Juventus and promoted strugglers Venezia will meet in Turin this weekend.

Having limped into the international break, Juve currently trail Italy's top six, while their Venetian visitors are stuck inside the drop zone despite finally posting a second win of the season.

The pressure is all on Juventus, who have consistently frittered away points with weak defending and wayward finishing.

Even so, the hosts should have too much nous and skill for a Venezia side that face an improbable fight for survival.

Aiming to pick up where they left off before the break, Bologna will host Serie A's bottom side when Udinese visit Stadio Dall'Ara on Sunday.

After a sticky start, both clubs have already changed coaches, and the Rossoblu's new boss has sparked a surge up the standings.

Bologna may be in fine form but they tend to falter on home turf, while Udinese are struggling to pick up points anywhere.

Only Sassuolo have conceded more goals than the Friulani, and the Rossoblu have kept just a single clean sheet, so a score-draw could be on the cards.

Roberto D'Aversa's Sassuolo tenure begins against Genoa on Sunday, with the Neroverdi in danger of slipping into the relegation zone.

The matchday 12 encounter pits two sides separated by four places in the Serie A table, with the higher-ranked Rossoblu chasing a fifth consecutive victory in this fixture.

Sassuolo's injury doubts complicate D'Aversa's first assignment, particularly with Berardi and Adzic potentially unavailable to bolster an attack already struggling to compensate for the team's defensive frailties.

Genoa arrive with fewer fitness concerns and a confident Osmajic, suggesting that De Rossi's men can secure a fifth successive victory over the Neroverdi.

After winning four of their last five Serie A matches, AC Milan will welcome promoted surprise package Frosinone to San Siro on Sunday.

While Milan inched into the top four before international football intervened, a famous win would see the Canarini move within one point of their hosts.

Both teams take a progressive approach, so it could be a wide-open contest at San Siro.

With more established stars and a much stronger bench, Milan should overcome their defensive frailties and ultimately come out on top.

> AC Milan vs. Frosinone preview.

Serie A's Sunday night showdown will see a battle of the Nerazzurri, as Atalanta BC welcome Inter Milan to Bergamo.

When the black-and-blue pair go toe to toe once again, the hosts hope to finally end an eight-year wait for victory over their regional rivals.

Inter have attempted the most shots in Serie A this season, they last failed to score in March, and their prolific talisman is set to make his long-awaited comeback.

That could mean trouble for Atalanta's fragile defence, so the hosts will suffer yet another defeat to their Nerazzurro neighbours.

NFL icon Tom Brady has purchased a small stake in Premier League giants Chelsea, according to ESPN.

It would see the seven-time Super Bowl champion make a swift return to investment in English football after he stepped away from Championship leaders Birmingham City earlier this month.

Brady was in attendance at the MetLife Stadium in Fresh Jersey when Chelsea beat Paris Saint-Germain 3-0 in the 2025 Club World Cup final.

The New England Patriots icon, who also owns a minority stake in the NFL's Las Vegas Raiders, reportedly has a good relationship with Behdad Eghbali, who oversees the club’s Clearlake Capital ownership.

Chelsea declined to comment when approached, but sources have stood up the negotiations.

It has been revealed that brady, the greatest quarterback of all time, secured a minority stake in Birmingham in August 2023. That followed Tom Wagner purchasing a 45 percent stake at the club earlier that same year.

NFL icon Tom Brady has purchased a small stake in Premier League giants Chelsea.

Brady watched Chelsea beat Paris Saint-Germain 3-0 in the 2025 Club World Cup final.

At Birmingham, Brady made headlines when he questioned Wayne Rooney’s work ethic during a documentary following his time at St Andrew’s.

Rooney, who went on to be sacked after just 15 games in charge, later described those comments as ‘very unfair’.

It has been revealed that when Brady exited Birmingham, the club noted in a statement: ‘Birmingham City Football Club expresses its sincere gratitude to Tom Brady for his involvement with and unwavering support for the club over the last three years. It was truly amazing to have someone with Tom’s experience and passion associated with the club, and the club looks forward to continuing to build on that foundation from the training ground to the Birmingham community.’.

Chelsea have invited minority shareholders with their women’s team.

NBA star Giannis Antetokounmpo previously purchased a stake in the side, partnering with Alexis Ohanian, the founder of social media platform Reddit who likewise invested in the team in 2025.

Serie A preview: AC Milan vs. Frosinone – Team news, opposition insight, stats and prediction

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1842 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sempremilan

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Milan will return to action on Sunday evening, hoping to pick up where they left off before the international break with a strong performance against Frosinone.
  • It has been revealed that if we look at the league, it has been a very decent start to the season for Ruben Amorim and his men.
  • Read SempreMilan ad-free and get access to exclusive news.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Milan will return to action on Sunday evening, hoping to pick up where they left off before the international break with a strong performance against Frosinone.

It has been revealed that if we look at the league, it has been a very decent start to the season for Ruben Amorim and his men. However, they are yet to win three games on the trot, so tomorrow’s encounter is a fantastic chance for them to really show their worth.

Read SempreMilan ad-free and get access to exclusive news. Click here for a free trial!

Recent findings suggest that it won’t be easy, though. Amorim stated during his press conference that it’s hard to identify the movement patterns of Frosinone, who certainly have the ability to make life difficult for the Rossoneri.

Game date: Sunday, November 22 Kick-off time: 18:00 (CET) Venue: San Siro Referee: Luca Pairetto (VAR: Pezzuto).

According to recent reports, some good news arrived on Saturday morning as Strahinja Pavlovic was deemed fit enough to be called up for the game. It’s not certain whether he will start or not, but Amorim at least mentioned that he’s happy to have the Serbian and ‘his fire’ back.

A few days ago, it was also confirmed that Mike Maignan will be at the manager’s disposal despite the injury scare with France. Of course, it’s not all perfect on the injury front as Matteo Gabbia, Fikayo Tomori, Ruben Loftus-Cheek, Alexis Saelemaekers and Samuel Chukwueze are still sidelined.

Recent findings suggest that anyway, moving on to the predicted starting eleven, it was initially thought that Amorim would field the same one as we saw against Genoa. However, he made it very clear during the presser that Musah won’t play as a left-back, so there will indeed be some changes.

According to the latest reports, the American will still start but in midfield instead, allowing Adrien Rabiot to have a slightly more advanced role. It also means that Davide Bartesaghi will come into the eleven, at the moment ahead of Pervis Estupinan in the race.

Alphadjo Cisse has been in red-hot form lately but it seems Amorim wants to manage expectations a little, with the youngster tipped to start on the bench. Christian Pulisic should thus have a role on the flank as opposed to in the centre, although one would imagine everything will be a bit fluid.

In a recent development, it’s no surprise to see that Goncalo Ramos should start up front, but of course, he will need to get going with the goalscoring sooner rather than later. Francesco Camarda is knocking on the door, as is Cisse who has been tested in that role before.

Predicted Milan XI (4-3-3): Maignan; Gila, De Winter, Diawara, Bartesaghi; Musah, Modric, Rabiot; Moreira, Ramos, Pulisic.

According to recent reports, predicted bench: Torriani, P. Terracciano, F. Terracciano, Pavlovic, Vladimirov, Estupinan, Jashari, Comotto, Hutchinson, Cisse, Camarda.

Injuries & suspensions: Gabbia, Tomori, Loftus-Cheek, Saelemaekers and Chukwueze.

Frosinone have definitely been one of the surprises of the season so far. After a very strong Serie B campaign with 81 points and only three games lost, they secured direct promotion to the top tier (finishing second) and have been making the most of the adventure.

They are presently on 20 points after eleven games, winning six, drawing two and losing three, which has put them in sixth place. That’s very strong for a newcomer and for a coach who is only in his second season with the club, especially considering the upset against Como.

Sources indicate that it’s the 56-year-old’s second attempt at Serie A after coaching Cremonese for half a season in 2022-23. He didn’t manage a single win then, so you can definitely say that the performance so far has been great revenge for him.

So, what is behind this rise? As pointed out by Gazzetta dello Sport, the direct style of play has been key for Frosinone. As opposed to Milan, who want to see a lot of the ball, they are willing to have less possession and break on the counter.

It has been revealed that it doesn’t mean that they sit back, though. In fact, it has been the opposite as they are the highest-pressing team in the league. The strategy thus seems to be to force mistakes out of the opponents, while also making sure that they are direct in possession.

According to recent reports, while collective effort deserves most of the praise, it has definitely helped that the likes of Giacomo Calo, Giorgi Kvernadze and Antonio Raimondo – among others – have performed at a very high level. They aren’t exactly big-name players, so a lot of them are having their breakout seasons.

According to recent reports, moving on to actual team news, the situation up front is not ideal for Frosinone as their top scorer, the aforementioned Antonio Raimondo, is out injured. Birigilea, who is on two goals, is set to replace him in the No.9 position.

Sources indicate that the Milan academy product Sebastiano Desplanches, who left the club four years ago, will be on the bench. He’s yet to make an appearance this season, with Alvini preferring Lorenzo Palmisani instead.

Predicted Frosinone XI (4-2-3-1): Palmisani; Oyono, Calvani, Monterisi, Terzic; Calo, Masini; Ghedjemis; Schmid, Kvernadze; Birigilea.

Predicted bench: Desplanches, Pisseri, Cittadini, Tchato, Amey, Akpoguma, Fayed, El Azzouzi, Cichella, Hasa, Fini, Zerbin, Bobcek.

Injuries & suspensions: Bracaglia, Grillitsch and Raimondo.

It has been revealed that this fixture has only been played six times, but even with such a small sample size, it’s clear that Milan are the favourites with four wins and two draws so far. They have won the last three as well, spread across the 2023-24 and 2018-19 seasons.

In a recent development, that said, the most recent encounter was a dramatic one, if you like. Olivier Giroud opened the scoring for Milan away from home but then Frosinone scored twice. Thanks to goals from Matteo Gabbia and Luka Jovic, the Rossoneri were able to turn it back in their favour.

The last time at San Siro, meanwhile, it was a great 3-1 win as Jovic, Pulisic and Tomori found the back of the net. Most of you will remember the American’s goal, as it was Maignan who assisted him with a fantastic pass.

➤ Milan are unbeaten in all six previous meetings against Frosinone in Serie A (W4 D2): among the teams against which they have never lost in the competition, the Rossoneri have played more games only against Pisa (14 – six also against Crotone and Lecco).

In a recent development, ➤ Milan have scored at least three goals in four of their six Serie A matches against Frosinone, producing 15 goals overall, an average of 2.5 per game. Only against Pescara (2.9) have they recorded a higher average, among the opponents they have faced on at least five occasions (2.5 also against Casale and Messina).

➤ Frosinone have won six games this season, drawing two and losing three. Only three newly promoted teams in the last 40 years have recorded more wins in their first 12 Serie A games of the season: Bari in 1994/95 (seven), Chievo in 2001/02 (seven), and Hellas Verona in 2013/14 (seven).

It has been revealed that ➤ Milan have won four of their last five league games (L1), scoring at least two goals in each, after failing to win three of their previous four (D3). The last time they scored more than one goal in consecutive Serie A matches was between September 2020 and January 2021, when they managed 15 games.

➤ Although Frosinone are unbeaten in three of their five away games this season (W1 D2), they have won just two of their last 27 away games in Serie A (including previous participations), with 10 draws and 15 defeats.

It has been revealed that ➤ Milan have failed to win four of their last seven Serie A games played after the international break (D2 L2). On the other hand, Frosinone are unbeaten in three of their last five top-flight matches immediately following Italy matches (W2 D1).

➤ Frosinone have attempted the most counterattacks from advantageous situations in Serie A this season: 22, almost double the number of any other team. On the other hand, Milan are the only team that haven’t allowed a single counterattack when trailing in the current campaign.

Sources indicate that ➤ Only Juventus (79) have attempted more long-range shots than Frosinone (77) this season. On the other hand, Milan are the team that have attempted the fewest shots from outside the area (30) and the one that have conceded the most shots from outside the area in relation to the total conceded, 44%.

➤ Adrien Rabiot has earned the most points for his team from direct goal contributions this season, having scored 10 goals and assisted four times. In the most recent matchday, he became the first Milan midfielder to be involved in at least one goal in six consecutive league appearances since Kaká in 2004 (who managed seven).

Industry observers note that ➤ Only Matías Soulé (80) has been involved in more sequences ending with a shot than Giacomo Calò (76) in this Serie A. The Frosinone player has scored five goals in the current campaign and only one midfielder has scored more goals in the first 12 matchdays in the top flight for a newly promoted team in the three points for a win era: Hidetoshi Nakata with Perugia in 1998/99 (six).

Industry observers note that since Frosinone like to play on the counterattacks, one player who I think could be crucial for Milan is Musah. As he’s set to start in midfield and not at left-back, the feeling is that his main role will be to prevent the opponents from having too much open space on the counter.

In a recent development, further up the pitch, I’m excited to see Moreira. He got himself a goal in Belgium’s win over Italy and he has looked a lot better on the right flank ever since the derby performance. He can definitely make the difference with his skill.

It has been revealed that as for Frosinone, it’s obvious that Calo is the man whom Milan will want to stop. He likes to dictate the play and if he’s allowed too much time on the ball, identifying his teammates in good positions, then there could be trouble for the Rossoneri.

Recent findings suggest that it will also be interesting to see if Birigilea can fill the shoes of Raimondo. He bagged a brace against Lecce but in the last two games, he failed to find the back of the net. He will surely be keen to get back on target.

Industry observers note that A lot of people are expecting this to be a high-scoring affair and that’s a very reasonable take, given how both teams play. That said, I think this could be one where Milan actually get their defence in order and don’t concede, even if that might be a somewhat optimistic prediction.

By Saikat Mandal | 22 Nov 2026 00:05, Last updated: 22 Nov 2026 00:05.

Today's La Liga predictions include a mouth-watering Camp Nou meeting between Barcelona and Villarreal, in addition to Getafe's 8pm kick-off against Atletico Madrid.

Barcelona will aim to post their 12th La Liga victory of the 2026-27 campaign when they resume their season at home to Villarreal on Sunday afternoon.

The Catalan giants did a league double over Villarreal last season, but each of the Yellow Submarine's last four successes over Barcelona have come on their travels.

Villarreal have enjoyed some recent away success over Barcelona and are capable of making this an uncomfortable match for the Catalan giants, but we are expecting Flick's team to navigate their way to another three points.

Both Racing de Santander and Real Sociedad will be aiming to make it back-to-back wins in Spain's top flight when they lock horns on Sunday afternoon.

Real Sociedad lead the overall head-to-head record between the two sides 49 wins to 34, while the Basque outfit have triumphed in the last three meetings.

Real Sociedad have lost three of their six away league matches this season, while Racing have been solid at home, so we are struggling to back a victory for the visitors and have instead settled on a low-scoring draw.

Sources indicate that > Racing de Santander vs. Real Sociedad.

Malaga's search for their first victory of the 2026-27 La Liga campaign will continue on Sunday, when they head to Estadio El Sadar to tackle Osasuna.

The White and Sky Blues are the only team in Spain's top flight yet to triumph this term, and they are in danger of becoming cut adrift at the bottom of the La Liga table.

We are expecting Malaga's winless run to continue this weekend, but the visitors have enough quality to secure a share of the spoils against an inconsistent Osasuna.

Atletico Madrid will be aiming to avoid a third straight defeat in all competitions when they continue their La Liga campaign against Getafe on Sunday.

This is a fixture that has been played on 47 occasions throughout history, with Atletico comfortably leading the overall head-to-head record 32 victories to Getafe's five.

Getafe have found it difficult to score this season, so we are backing Atletico to keep a clean sheet in a much-needed victory on Sunday.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • Cristiano Ronaldo may have finally departed the international stage, but he still remained a major part of Portugal's story over the past week.
  • That came after they suffered a humiliating 4-1 defeat by Denmark in the first game since his retirement, their heaviest home loss in competitive history.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

By WILL PICKWORTH, SPORTS REPORTER.

Published: 02:00 EST, 21 November 2026 | Updated: 04:21 EST, 21 November 2026.

Cristiano Ronaldo may have finally departed the international stage, but he still remained a major part of Portugal's story over the past week.

That came after they suffered a humiliating 4-1 defeat by Denmark in the first game since his retirement, their heaviest home loss in competitive history.

In the aftermath of that match, Ronaldo's mother Dolores introduced a furious and unprompted attack on the national team, claiming the defeat was just, and added she was happy to see the result.

Despite an emotional and historic tribute to Ronaldo pre-game, Dolores also expressed her unhappiness at what had unfolded, before she claimed the veteran's former international team-mates failed to show him the respect he deserved during his career.

Dolores has not always been an outspoken presence over the years, but has often stepped up to defend her son when she feels necessary.

So, in light of her outburst, Daily Mail Sport has taken a look at other examples of when the mums of footballers have got involved in their careers.

Cristiano Ronaldo's mum became embroiled in her son's row with Portugal's national team after saying she was happy to see them suffer a heavy defeat (Source: Instagram/doloresaveiroofficial).

Veronique Rabiot – Adrien Rabiot.

Adrien Rabiot's mother Veronique has developed a reputation as an uncompromising and fiercely protective negotiator in her role as his agent.

This has seen the French midfielder face several flashpoints in his career, beginning  when Veronique pulled him out of Man City's academy after just six months in 2008 because she felt they were not looking after his interests like they should be.

During his time at PSG, where Rabiot ultimately broke through and spent seven seasons in the first team, Veronique then frequently clashed with the club's hierarchy.

Potential transfers to Roma and Man United during his career have also both collapsed late on, a factor some reports attach to Veronique's role in the deals.

There have been several notable flashpoints on the international stage too, not least when she backed her son's controversial decision to withdraw from France's standby list for the 2018 World Cup.

But that was nothing compared to the aftermath of France's shock exit from Euro 2020 at the last-16 stage.

Veronique made headlines at the time for engaging in a heated confrontation with the parents of Kylian Mbappe and the entourage of Paul Pogba in the stands over on-pitch errors and perceived arrogance during Les Bleus' campaign.

Adrien Rabiot's mother Veronique (centre) has developed a reputation as a formidable force.

As the mother of one of the best footballers on the planet, Fayza Lamari was always likely to be a major powerbroker, and she has played a key role in Kylian Mbappe's career, acting as his chief negotiator and business manager.

This has seen Fayza oversee Mbappe's commercial obligations and image rights, while she played a central role in his dramatic contract extension at PSG in 2022.

She was similarly vital when Mbappe joined Real Madrid in 2024. On that occasion, she was credited for helping to secure a huge signing bonus and favourable image rights split for her son.

Fayza hasn't been afraid to publicly stand up for the forward, and she was key in the legal dispute over unpaid salary and bonuses that he felt he was owed by PSG after his exit.

PSG were ultimately ordered to pay Mbappe €60million (£52.5m) by a French court in a major victory for Fayza.

Kylian Mbappe's mum Fayza (also pictured with his brother Ethan) has played a key role in the commercial side of his career.

Sheila Ebana has been a foundational and supportive presence throughout Lamine Yamal's childhood and rise into professional football.

But, alongside regularly attending Yamal's games, Sheila has become a celebrity in her own right after embracing her public profile.

She regularly provides an insight into her life and shares behind the scenes clips with Yamal and his half brother Keyne on social media, racking up 2.8million followers on Instagram and 2.6million on TikTok.

Sheila has also regularly made paid appearances and attended VIP events, including a bizarre Christmas gala dinner that Daily Mail Sport went to in November 2025 where members of the public paid hundreds of pounds for a three-course meal, champagne, entertainment and a meet-and-greet.

To demonstrate how Sheila has embraced her fame, she once responded to online critics by retorting: 'I don't just think I'm famous - I am.'.

Lamine Yamal's mum (pictured below together with his half-brother Keyne) has embraced her celebrity fame.

Denise Bellingham – Jude Bellingham.

Jude Bellingham has often credited his mother Denise for helping to manage his life off the pitch and keep him grounded.

When he moved to Germany to join Borussia Dortmund as a 17-year-old, Denise went with him – before subsequently following the midfielder to Spain after his transfer to Real Madrid – while his father Mark stayed with his brother Jobe.

She is understood to handle his domestic affairs and finances, while Bellingham inadvertently revealed during the 2022 World Cup that she still made his bed.

Denise has generally provided a constant source of advice, logistical support – which has included driving him to training in the past – and organisational help throughout his time in the game.

The England star is clearly appreciative of all she has done, describing her as his 'queen' and 'backbone', and crediting her with helping to keep him level headed throughout the highs and lows of his career.

Jude Bellingham (pictured also with dad Mark and brother Jobe) has described his mum Denise as his 'queen' and 'backbone'.

Marcia Lewis – Myles Lewis-Skelly.

Myles Lewis-Skelly's mother Marcia Lewis has played a crucial role in his rise into Arsenal and England's first team.

When Lewis-Skelly entered the Arsenal academy system at the age of eight, Marcia wanted to learn more about football to ensure she could protect and guide her son's progression.

She subsequently qualified as an agent, meaning she now represents Lewis-Skelly, and also enrolled in a Master's degree in Football Business.

Marcia has since taken part in contract negotiations and filtered external pressures away from her son during his development.

She was later inspired to set up the No1Fan.club, a platform that aims to support families who have children in academy football.

The outlet is dedicated to helping navigate various challenges that arise, such as dealing with scouts, agents and the general pressures associated with youth football.

Myles Lewis-Skelly's mum Marcia Lewis tried to learn more about the business of football so she would be able to support her son on his journey (Source: Instagram/myleslewisskelly).

Harry Maguire's mother Zoe has taken a more low-profile approach to her son's career than others, yet she has never been afraid to speak out when she feels the need to.

This included back in 2023 when she snapped after years of watching her son face significant abuse, both online and in stadiums.

At the time, Zoe labelled the heat on the defender as 'disgraceful' and 'unacceptable', and stated it went 'far beyond' football.

She re-emerged into the public eye three years later when Maguire was snubbed from England's World Cup squad.

After that, she tweeted: 'Absolutely disgusted.'.

In another post addressing Maguire, she added: 'You couldn’t have done anymore. Hold your head high …Disgraceful.'.

Arsenal 1-0 Hull: Not efficient, but enough

📅 08 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (726 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Arseblog

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, in yesterday’s preview blog, I spoke about Arsenal’s attacking efficiency, and how that might be key to taking all three points.
  • According to recent reports, despite generally dominating possession, I thought there was a lack of precision in certain aspects of our first half play.
  • It’s fair to say Hull didn’t leave a lot of room behind a defensive line that often had six players stretched across it, but late in the half a superb Martin Odegaard pass sent him clean through, one on one with the keeper.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, in yesterday’s preview blog, I spoke about Arsenal’s attacking efficiency, and how that might be key to taking all three points. In yesterday’s game against Hull, Arsenal took 21 shots, 10 of which were on target, and scored one goal from that. Efficient?

According to recent reports, despite generally dominating possession, I thought there was a lack of precision in certain aspects of our first half play. Passes weren’t quite quick enough or accurate enough, but there were moments when we could have found the breakthrough. Gabriel almost got on the end of a Noni Madueke cross which was flicked on towards the back post, Rice had a tame shot from a free kick before a late header which he probably should have done better with.

And then there was Kai Havertz. It’s fair to say Hull didn’t leave a lot of room behind a defensive line that often had six players stretched across it, but late in the half a superb Martin Odegaard pass sent him clean through, one on one with the keeper. I haven’t seen replays but in real time I felt like he should have pulled the trigger – instead he over-complicated it. You have to be prepared to shoot from there, even if it’s on your wrong foot.

Then there was a penalty incident when he complained vociferously, play went on, the ref was then told to go to the screen and we all assumed it would be a penalty. However, the ref said it was a foul but Havertz was offside – and it felt like a massive waste of time. Afterwards, it emerged it should have been a penalty, but apparently the rule is ‘open to interpretation’. So clear as mud then.

According to recent reports, in the second half, we seemed to play down our right a lot, with Madueke the outlet most of the time. I thought he did pretty well, much better than Christos Tzolis on the other side, but the breakthrough wouldn’t come. Mikel Merino replaced Rice (who seemed to be on the end of a wild challenge in midfield that the ref just ignored as he tumbled through the air), and Viktor Gyokeres came on for Havertz.

Industry observers note that on 71 minutes though, we found the goal. Madueke’s shot was spilled by the keeper, Odegaard was quickest to react to poke the ball home for 1-0. And to be fair, you always felt confident that would be enough. We are the masters of the single goal margin win, and this was another one. Not a day that will live long in the memory or anything, but a 1-0 win that takes us into the Interlull in really good shape, and there’s not much arguing with that.

Or really, much more to say about this game. Mikel Arteta sounded happy enough, saying:.

According to recent reports, I’m delighted with the win. To go into the international break with a win is one of the best things about being a coach or player, I would say. Regarding the performance, I thought we were the better team, had enough chances to score and make it bigger for ourselves and we weren’t efficient enough to take them.

Recent findings suggest that we then had to rely on generating volume, plenty of persisting until we finally broke them down. Martin then got the goal. Not the most beautiful one, but the most effective one, a simple ‘shoot and then follow the next action’, and that was ultimately enough to win the game.

In a recent development, so Arsenal sit top of the table, with 9 wins from 10 so far this season in the league, and it’s a very impressive run of form. Do I wish we had more attacking potency?
